meta.blurb: Ravi teaches all day and lies awake at night, with a body like an alarm nobody can switch off. Over one busy week he learns what stress does inside us, then tries calming tools that have real evidence behind them.
meta.bible: Ravi: a school teacher in his thirties, hard-working and a little anxious, who learns about stress over one busy week. The book explains the stress response in plain words and then teaches calming tools in three parts: Body, Mind and Life. The week runs from Sunday night to Friday; the plan is made on Saturday; the tools are tried over the weeks that follow; the last chapter is a Monday a month later. People: Meera is Ravi's older sister, a nurse who works night shifts and gives general information only, never a diagnosis; Tom teaches maths and is calm under pressure; Mrs Hale is the head teacher; Sam is a pupil in Ravi's class, Class Seven B, who asks good questions; Dev is Ravi's old friend and Biscuit is Dev's dog; Dr Reyes is the doctor Ravi sees at the end; the school has an inspection on Thursday and parents' evening on Wednesday. Key terms: CBT, Stressor, Stressors, Amygdala, Adrenaline, Cortisol, Eustress, Chronic, Hormone, Hormones, Mindfulness, Resilience, Caffeine, Alcohol, Vagus, Nervous, Cognitive, Behavioural, Therapy, Therapies, Crisis, Helpline, Immune, Digestion, Nausea, Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Hippocampus, Prefrontal, Cortex, Pituitary, Adrenal, Glucose, Sympathetic, Parasympathetic, Melatonin, Insomnia, Anxiety, Depression, Burnout, Counsellor, Psychologist, Progressive, Yoga, Tai, Chi, Nicotine, Eczema, Catastrophising, Rumination, Circadian, Endorphins, Gratitude, Assertive, Hypertension, Irritable, Bowel, Syndrome, Inflammation, Steroid. Facts: adrenaline comes first and cortisol follows more slowly, both made by the adrenal glands above the kidneys; the stress response is useful in short bursts and harmful when it never switches off; the word stress comes from engineering, where it means a force pressing on a beam or bridge; the amygdala is a small almond-shaped region, one on each side of the brain; cortisol is highest in the early morning and lowest around midnight; evidence for blood pressure, immunity, breathing exercises, nature, writing and mindfulness is real but modest, and the book says so; no single food, drink or supplement is proven to cure stress; burnout is described by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon from long-lasting work stress that has not been managed. Voice and tone: calm, kind, plain and a little humorous; never alarming. Nobody gets personal medical advice; the book gives general information and tells readers to see a doctor about their own health. Beat 196 gives crisis advice: contact emergency services or a helpline. This book is general information and is not medical advice.
chapters: The Smoke Alarm in the Brain

beats.scene: Ravi lies awake in a dark bedroom, one hand on his chest
beats.summary: On Sunday night Ravi lies awake while his heart pounds for no clear reason.

beats.scene: A clock showing midnight beside a list of the week's tasks
beats.summary: Ravi runs through the week ahead and sees why his mind will not rest.

beats.scene: Ravi in the kitchen with a glass of water and a pile of marking
beats.summary: Ravi goes to the kitchen for water and finds his marking still waiting.

beats.scene: Ravi studies a calendar with tired faces drawn on it
beats.summary: Ravi realises that he has felt this way, in small ways, for months.

beats.scene: A phone lights up on the kitchen table with a message from Meera
beats.summary: Ravi's sister Meera, a nurse on a night shift, texts him on her break.

beats.scene: Ravi reads Meera's reply on his phone, looking a little relieved
beats.summary: Meera says a racing heart at night is common, and she gives general information only.

beats.scene: A friendly nurse in uniform smiles at a phone on a hospital ward
beats.summary: Meera says his body is not broken; it is doing an old job too well.

beats.scene: Ravi opens a new notebook and writes a title on the first page
beats.summary: Ravi starts a notebook headed with the question, what is my body doing?

beats.scene: Ravi writes a plan on a notebook page with a mug of tea
beats.summary: Ravi decides to spend one busy week learning how stress works.

beats.scene: Ravi sleeps at last as grey morning light reaches the window
beats.summary: Ravi finally falls asleep a few hours before his alarm goes off.

beats.scene: Ravi stands on a crowded bus on Monday morning, holding a coffee
beats.summary: On Monday morning Ravi squeezes onto a crowded bus and feels the old tension return.

beats.scene: Ravi and Tom talk over mugs in a busy staff room
beats.summary: Tom, a colleague, jokes about Ravi's tired face and Ravi asks what stress even is.

beats.scene: A drawing of a bridge with arrows pressing down on its beam
beats.summary: The word stress comes from engineering, where it means a force pressing on a beam or bridge.

beats.scene: Ravi writes two columns headed demand and response in his notebook
beats.summary: A stressor is the demand; the stress response is what the body does about it.

beats.scene: Four small drawings: a hot sun, a deadline, a quarrel and a wedding
beats.summary: Stressors come in many kinds, from heat and pain to deadlines, quarrels and even happy events.

beats.scene: A cutaway drawing of a head with a small almond shape glowing deep inside
beats.summary: Deep in the brain sits the amygdala, a small almond-shaped region that watches for danger.

beats.scene: A figure jumps back from a garden hose, an arrow showing a brain shortcut
beats.summary: Some signals seem to take a quick shortcut to the amygdala, so the body can react before the mind has thought.

beats.scene: A drawing of the hypothalamus as a control room above the brain stem
beats.summary: The hypothalamus works like a control room, linking the brain to the body's nerves and hormones.

beats.scene: A calm figure behind the forehead presses a brake lever on a small alarm
beats.summary: The thinking front of the brain can calm a false alarm, but it works slowly and tires easily.

beats.scene: Ravi looks up in surprise as a loud bell sounds above a classroom door
beats.summary: At two o'clock the fire bell rings, and Ravi's heart leaps before he has had time to think.

beats.scene: Children line up by the classroom door as a fire bell rings
beats.summary: The fire drill begins, and Ravi's body reacts before his thoughts catch up.

beats.scene: A drawing of a body with a fast heart, quick lungs and sweaty palms
beats.summary: Within seconds his heart speeds up, his breathing quickens and his palms turn damp.

beats.scene: A drawing of the two adrenal glands sitting on top of the kidneys
beats.summary: Adrenaline is a hormone, a chemical messenger made in two small adrenal glands above the kidneys.

beats.scene: A nerve carries a lightning signal from the brain to a gland
beats.summary: Nerves carry the order to the adrenal glands in seconds; this is the body's accelerator, the sympathetic system.

beats.scene: A heart pumping red arrows toward two arms and two legs
beats.summary: The heart beats faster and harder to send blood to the muscles, and the lungs take in more air.

beats.scene: An eye with a wide pupil, an ear and a drop of sweat
beats.summary: Pupils widen, hearing sharpens and sweat appears, which cools a body that is about to work hard.

beats.scene: A liver pours a glittering stream of sugar into a blood vessel
beats.summary: Adrenaline also tells the liver to release glucose, a quick fuel for the muscles and the brain.

beats.scene: Ravi leads the line out into the playground while one pupil stands frozen
beats.summary: Ravi leads his class out calmly; one child freezes, which is also a normal response to alarm.

beats.scene: The whole school stands in neat rows on the playground in the sun
beats.summary: After the all clear, Ravi's hands still shake, because adrenaline takes several minutes to fade.

beats.scene: Sam points at Ravi's hands while the class settles down at their desks
beats.summary: Sam asks why Ravi's hands are shaking, and Ravi realises that explaining stress is the best way to learn it.

beats.scene: Ravi at his kitchen table reads handwritten notes sent by Meera
beats.summary: On Monday evening Meera sends notes: adrenaline is the sprinter and cortisol the long-distance runner.

beats.scene: A brain, a pea-sized gland below it, and two glands above kidneys
beats.summary: If danger lasts, the brain uses a second, slower route through the pituitary gland to the adrenal glands.

beats.scene: A clock with a rising curve drawn beside it, peaking at thirty minutes
beats.summary: The adrenal glands release cortisol, which rises over minutes and takes an hour or more to fade.

beats.scene: A glowing battery being charged beside a drop of blood and a flame
beats.summary: Cortisol raises blood sugar, supports blood pressure and keeps the body going for longer.

beats.scene: A shield labelled life next to a small bottle of cortisol
beats.summary: Cortisol is not an enemy: people whose bodies make too little become seriously ill.

beats.scene: A sun rises above a curve that is high at dawn
beats.summary: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: highest in the early morning and lowest around midnight.

beats.scene: A thermostat dial on a wall next to a brain and a hormone drop
beats.summary: Cortisol also sends a message back to the brain to turn the alarm down, like a thermostat.

beats.scene: A drawn vagus nerve running from the brain to the heart and the gut
beats.summary: Once the danger passes, the calming system takes over; its main wire is the vagus nerve.

beats.scene: A pause button pressed over drawings of a stomach, a seedling and a mouth
beats.summary: While the alarm is on, the body pauses jobs that can wait, such as digestion and repair.

beats.scene: Ravi's notebook page with a two-column chart of fast and slow messengers
beats.summary: Ravi sums up: adrenaline is fast and brief, cortisol is slow and lasting, and both should switch off again.

beats.scene: Ravi stands calmly at the front of a school hall before a morning assembly
beats.summary: On Tuesday Ravi gives a short assembly and notices that his nerves make him sharper.

beats.scene: A sprinter crouches at the start line with a stopwatch beside her
beats.summary: A short burst of stress can sharpen focus, speed up reactions and give extra energy.

beats.scene: A small plant reaching up toward the sun beside the word eustress
beats.summary: Helpful stress has a name, eustress, from the Greek for good; a challenge can feel exciting.

beats.scene: A hill-shaped curve drawn on a whiteboard, with three smiling and frowning faces
beats.summary: Too little pressure bores us and too much overwhelms us; the best performance is often in the middle.

beats.scene: Ravi's marking diary, with one calm day and one crowded day side by side
beats.summary: Ravi sees that he spends most days far over the top of the curve.

beats.scene: A mountain of tangled red threads beside a single smooth thread
beats.summary: Stress turns harmful when it lasts for weeks or months without time to recover; that is called chronic stress.

beats.scene: A phone, a laptop and a crowded train showing many small alarms at once
beats.summary: Modern life brings stress that lasts, such as emails, noise, money worries and commutes, and we cannot run away.

beats.scene: A watchdog barks at a laptop showing a full inbox
beats.summary: The body cannot tell a growl from an angry email very well, because the same machinery answers both.

beats.scene: A car engine revving red-hot in a driveway with nobody inside
beats.summary: A system built for sprints cannot run a marathon without wear; the cost builds up like a revving engine.

beats.scene: Ravi writes the word recovery in large letters in his notebook
beats.summary: Ravi writes that recovery is part of the job, and wonders what long stress does to the body.

beats.scene: Ravi slumps at the breakfast table on Wednesday morning with a heavy head
beats.summary: On Wednesday Ravi wakes after about five hours of sleep and feels heavy and slow.

beats.scene: A checklist with tired eyes, a headache, a sore neck and a short temper
beats.summary: Common signs of long-lasting stress include poor sleep, tiredness, headaches, aches and a short temper.

beats.scene: A person hunched at a laptop with shoulders raised and jaw clenched
beats.summary: Under stress, muscles tense, especially in the neck, shoulders and jaw.

beats.scene: A drawing of a head with a tight band squeezing across the forehead
beats.summary: Tension headaches are common and linked with tight muscles in the neck and scalp; most are harmless.

beats.scene: A man rubbing his lower back beside a stack of books
beats.summary: Stress does not make pain imaginary, but it can make real aches and back pain feel worse.

beats.scene: Ravi lies awake in bed, a clock reading three in the morning
beats.summary: Stress and sleep trouble feed each other: an alert body is hard to put to sleep, and poor sleep adds stress.

beats.scene: A tired person with a battery icon showing a very low charge
beats.summary: A body running its alarm uses up energy, so long stress often brings deep tiredness, which has many other possible causes too.

beats.scene: A coffee cup, biscuits and a phone on a desk at night
beats.summary: Stress also changes habits: some people eat more, some less, drink more coffee and move less.

beats.scene: A hand scratching an itchy red patch on an arm beside a calendar
beats.summary: For some people, skin conditions such as eczema or acne flare during stressful times.

beats.scene: Ravi and Meera look at a notebook page headed notice, do not diagnose
beats.summary: Meera warns that these signs are not a diagnosis, because they have many causes, so Ravi starts a stress diary to notice patterns.

beats.scene: Ravi checks his pulse with two fingers outside a classroom before parents' evening
beats.summary: Before parents' evening on Wednesday, Ravi's heart is pounding, and he checks his pulse.

beats.scene: A drawing of a heart with a rising pressure gauge beside it
beats.summary: In stress the heart rate and blood pressure rise, which is normal and healthy for a short time.

beats.scene: A graph of a pressure line that stays high, with a doctor's question mark
beats.summary: Over years, repeated surges and unhealthy habits are linked with higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease.

beats.scene: A pharmacist wraps a blood pressure cuff around a customer's arm
beats.summary: High blood pressure cannot be felt, but it is easy to measure; a doctor or nurse can explain the numbers.

beats.scene: A gut with tiny nerve cells and a thread leading to the brain
beats.summary: The gut has its own network of nerve cells and talks with the brain, so stress can cause butterflies, nausea and cramps.

beats.scene: A sleeping stomach and a hand holding a hot cup of herbal tea
beats.summary: Stress can make conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome worse, which does not mean they are all in the mind.

beats.scene: A drawing of tiny white blood cells guarding a small cut on a finger
beats.summary: Short-term stress can boost parts of the immune system, but long-term stress is linked with weaker defences and slower healing.

beats.scene: A set of kitchen scales balancing a sweet cake against a tape measure
beats.summary: Long-term stress is linked in some studies with higher blood sugar and with fat stored around the middle.

beats.scene: Ravi sits relieved at a desk beneath a banner reading the body repairs
beats.summary: The damage is neither instant nor fixed: many effects ease when stress eases, which relieves Ravi.

beats.scene: Ravi walks home under a street light after the last parent has left
beats.summary: Ravi gets through parents' evening with slow breaths and walks home at ten, wondering about his mind.

beats.scene: Ravi searches a messy desk on Thursday morning for a missing lesson plan
beats.summary: On inspection day Ravi cannot find his lesson plan and blanks on a pupil's name.

beats.scene: A head with a narrow torch beam and darkness all around
beats.summary: Stress narrows attention to the threat, which helps in danger but makes broad, flexible thinking harder.

beats.scene: A small notepad with only a few lines of space, crowded with worries
beats.summary: Working memory is like a small notepad; worry fills it, leaving less room to think.

beats.scene: A drawing of a seahorse-shaped brain region labelled memory
beats.summary: Long periods of high stress hormones have been linked with trouble forming and recalling memories, and this is often reversible.

beats.scene: A drawing of a forehead region dimmed while an alarm region glows brightly
beats.summary: Under pressure the planning part of the brain works less well, so we fall back on habit and find decisions harder.

beats.scene: A thundercloud over a small figure beside a spinning thought
beats.summary: Stress can bring irritability, tearfulness, feeling flat, and spinning worries; it can feed anxiety and low mood, though they are not the same thing.

beats.scene: Ravi stands over Sam's desk, both looking uncomfortable after a sharp word
beats.summary: Ravi snaps at Sam, regrets it at once, and apologises the next minute.

beats.scene: A drawing of a candle burning low beside three words: exhaustion, distance, doubt
beats.summary: Burnout is described by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon from long, unmanaged work stress: exhaustion, distance and less effectiveness.

beats.scene: A seedling pushing up through grey soil with a small sun above
beats.summary: The good news: many changes seen in long stress seem to ease with rest and time.

beats.scene: A kind inspector shakes Ravi's hand at the classroom door as the sun sets
beats.summary: The inspection goes well; at five Ravi collapses into a chair and sees he has been in alarm mode for months.

beats.scene: Ravi and Tom eat lunch on a bench on Friday in the school garden
beats.summary: On Friday Ravi asks why Tom, facing the same inspection, stayed so relaxed.

beats.scene: Two climbers face the same steep cliff, one smiling and one worried
beats.summary: The same event can feel like a challenge to one person and a threat to another.

beats.scene: A balance scale with demands on one side and resources on the other
beats.summary: Stress tends to rise when we feel that the demands are greater than our resources.

beats.scene: Ravi at a whiteboard writing a list headed things I can decide
beats.summary: Having some control makes stress easier to bear, so Ravi lists what he can decide.

beats.scene: A weekly timetable pinned to a wall with a green tick beside each day
beats.summary: Knowing what to expect makes stress easier, while surprises keep the alarm primed.

beats.scene: Three friends sit close together on a sofa with mugs, one speaking softly
beats.summary: Support from other people softens stress, while loneliness makes it harder.

beats.scene: A baby, a teenager and an adult, each with a different-sized alarm bell
beats.summary: People differ: genes, early life experience, sleep and health all shape how strongly the alarm reacts, and it is no weakness.

beats.scene: A woman lies in bed imagining a stormy sea of future problems
beats.summary: The mind can sound the alarm for things that have not happened, or replay old ones, and the body reacts almost as if they were real.

beats.scene: A person holds a set of levers labelled body, mind and life
beats.summary: Because thoughts and habits matter, there are levers we can pull on the body, the mind and the life around us.

beats.scene: Ravi at a desk on Friday evening, writing three words on three index cards
beats.summary: On Friday night Ravi writes Body, Mind and Life on three cards, ending his week of learning.

beats.scene: Three index cards labelled body, mind and life lie on a sunny desk
beats.summary: On Saturday morning Ravi spreads the three cards on his desk and plans the reset.

beats.scene: Meera arrives at the door holding a paper bag of croissants
beats.summary: Meera visits with croissants and warns that there is no magic fix.

beats.scene: A pile of scientific papers beside a large and a small plus sign
beats.summary: Studies compare groups and measure average effects; modest effects are not useless.

beats.scene: A three-step staircase labelled strong, modest and mixed evidence
beats.summary: Meera sorts the tools: strong evidence for exercise, talking therapies and sleep habits; modest for breathing, mindfulness and nature; mixed for writing.

beats.scene: A wavy line that rises and falls and settles back to a flat baseline
beats.summary: The aim is not zero stress but to let the alarm switch off when the danger passes and to lower the baseline.

beats.scene: A scientist's tray with three small test tubes, one marked keep, one marked drop
beats.summary: Try one thing at a time, keep what helps, drop what does not, and expect results to differ from person to person.

beats.scene: A diary page with a row of numbers from zero to ten
beats.summary: Ravi starts a stress diary, scoring each evening from zero to ten and noting one line about the day.

beats.scene: A doctor's bag with a small red cross beside a diary
beats.summary: Meera's safety note: the tools are for everyday stress, and chest pain, fainting or breathlessness need checking by a doctor.

beats.scene: A calm figure sits upright, one hand on the belly
beats.summary: Body first, because the body is the quickest door: you can often calm the body before you can calm the thoughts.

beats.scene: Ravi puts the Body card on top of the pile at sunset
beats.summary: Ravi puts the Body card on top of the pile and plans to begin on Monday.

beats.scene: Ravi sits on a chair with one hand on his belly
beats.summary: Meera shows Ravi that breathing is the one automatic function we can also control.

beats.scene: Two chests, one breathing quickly and high, one slowly and low
beats.summary: In stress we breathe fast and high in the chest; calm breathing is slower and lower, into the belly.

beats.scene: A heart-rate wave that dips slightly as an arrow points down at each out-breath
beats.summary: Breathing out slows the heart a little, so a long out-breath is a way to nudge the brake.

beats.scene: A vagus nerve glowing softly from the brain to the heart
beats.summary: Slow breathing may stimulate the vagus nerve and the calming system, although the exact mechanism is still being studied.

beats.scene: A diagram of a four-count in-breath and a six-count out-breath
beats.summary: Try breathing in through the nose for a count of four and out slowly for a count of six, for a few minutes.

beats.scene: A square with four equal sides labelled in, hold, out, hold
beats.summary: Another pattern is square breathing: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four.

beats.scene: A small stack of study papers beside a gentle downward arrow
beats.summary: Small studies suggest slow breathing can lower blood pressure a little and ease anxiety, but the effect is modest and it is not a cure.

beats.scene: A dizzy figure stops beside a gentle caution sign and a lung
beats.summary: Do not force it or hold the breath for long; stop if dizzy, and people with lung or heart conditions or pregnancy should ask a doctor first.

beats.scene: Ravi breathes slowly at a bus stop, a rainy street behind him
beats.summary: Practise when calm, like a fire drill, so the tool is ready when stress arrives.

beats.scene: Sam spills a pot of blue paint across a desk and Ravi stays steady
beats.summary: When Sam knocks over a pot of paint, Ravi breathes out slowly and his heart settles; it is not magic, but it helps.

beats.scene: Meera shows Ravi how to clench a fist on a sofa, then open it
beats.summary: Meera teaches progressive muscle relaxation, invented about a hundred years ago: tense, then release.

beats.scene: Ravi lies on a mat and curls his toes tightly
beats.summary: Start with the feet: tense for about five seconds, release for ten to twenty, and notice the difference.

beats.scene: A drawn body with arrows moving from the feet up through each muscle group
beats.summary: Move upwards through calves, thighs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders and face, one group at a time.

beats.scene: A hand slowly opens, with small arrows showing the muscles letting go
beats.summary: Many people do not notice how tense they are until the muscles let go; the contrast teaches the body what relaxed feels like.

beats.scene: A small stack of studies next to a smiling figure on a sofa
beats.summary: Studies suggest the method can ease tension and anxiety to a moderate degree, but it takes practice.

beats.scene: Ravi at his desk drops his shoulders and unclenches his teeth
beats.summary: A short desk version: drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, let the tongue rest and breathe out.

beats.scene: Ravi gently rolls his neck by the classroom window
beats.summary: Gentle stretches such as neck rolls and a doorway chest stretch can ease stiffness; stop if there is pain.

beats.scene: A class of adults stand on mats in a bright room, stretching slowly
beats.summary: Yoga and tai chi join gentle movement to breathing; studies suggest modest benefits for stress and mood.

beats.scene: A warm bath with steam and a folded towel beside a candle
beats.summary: Warmth, such as a bath or a heat pad on the neck, relaxes muscles; it costs little and feels good.

beats.scene: Ravi lies in bed, eyes closed, as moonlight shines through the curtain
beats.summary: At bedtime Ravi does a slow body scan, from toes to head, and falls asleep halfway; he decides that counts.

beats.scene: Ravi walks briskly along a tree-lined street after school
beats.summary: Meera says stress prepares the body to move, so movement helps finish the cycle; Ravi takes an after-school walk.

beats.scene: A runner, a cyclist and a dancer in a row under a bright sky
beats.summary: Regular activity is linked with lower anxiety and better mood, and endorphins are often credited, though scientists are still working out the full story.

beats.scene: A calendar with a few short walks marked in bright green
beats.summary: Adults are often advised to aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, but any amount helps and short walks count.

beats.scene: Ravi dances in his kitchen with a wooden spoon for a microphone
beats.summary: It need not mean a gym: stairs, dancing, cycling, gardening and playing with children all count.

beats.scene: Ravi walks under tall trees as the sun sets orange behind the leaves
beats.summary: At sunset he counts his steps to a gentle rhythm and the walk starts to quieten the mind.

beats.scene: A bench among green trees, with a bird and a stream
beats.summary: Time in green places is linked with lower stress and, in some studies, lower cortisol, though the effect is modest.

beats.scene: A person gazes at a gentle river as leaves float past
beats.summary: One idea is that nature holds attention gently without demanding it, which lets tired focus rest.

beats.scene: A sun rising over rooftops while a person stands at an open window
beats.summary: Morning daylight helps set the body clock, so a short walk in the morning can help sleep later on.

beats.scene: A tired runner sits on a step with a water bottle
beats.summary: Too much exercise adds stress, so rest days matter; listen to the body, and ask a doctor first if you have a heart condition.

beats.scene: Ravi and three colleagues walk in a line around the school field at lunchtime
beats.summary: Tom invites Ravi to a lunchtime walking group, and three colleagues join them around the field.

beats.scene: Ravi stares at the ceiling at two in the morning, a moon outside
beats.summary: Ravi sees how sleep and stress feed each other, after another night of five hours.

beats.scene: A brain sweeping a floor with a bucket of tiny memory stars beside it
beats.summary: Sleep helps memory, repair and emotional processing; adults generally need about seven to nine hours, with variation.

beats.scene: A small alarm bell glowing brighter beside a bed with rumpled sheets
beats.summary: After a poor night, studies suggest the brain's alarm reacts more strongly, so small problems feel bigger.

beats.scene: A clock showing the same wake-up time on both a weekday and a Sunday
beats.summary: A steady wake-up time, even at weekends, helps the body clock to settle into a rhythm.

beats.scene: Ravi puts his marking bag in a cupboard in the evening light
beats.summary: A wind-down hour with dimmer lights and no work helps the mind shift from day to night.

beats.scene: A phone placed face down in a drawer beside a small lamp
beats.summary: Phones keep the mind busy; the evidence on blue light is mixed, but stimulating content matters, so keep the phone out of the bedroom.

beats.scene: A dark, cool bedroom with a bed, a curtain and pillows
beats.summary: A cool, dark, quiet room helps; if awake for a long time, get up and do something calm until sleepy.

beats.scene: A page of a notebook with a short list headed tomorrow beside a pillow
beats.summary: Before bed, writing a short to-do list for tomorrow may help the mind let go of worries; one small study found people fell asleep faster.

beats.scene: A figure in bed breathes slowly beside a turned-away clock
beats.summary: If you wake in the night, do not watch the clock; breathe slowly, rest and remember that one bad night is not a disaster.

beats.scene: Ravi smiles at his diary, which shows a column of lower numbers
beats.summary: If trouble sleeping lasts for weeks, see a doctor; a talking therapy for insomnia is well supported, and Ravi's sleep slowly improves.

beats.scene: A table with five empty coffee cups, a wine glass and crisps
beats.summary: Ravi counts his habits: five coffees a day, wine on Fridays and lunch from a machine.

beats.scene: A coffee bean and a drawing of a brain with a sleepy signal blocked
beats.summary: Caffeine is a stimulant that blocks the brain's tiredness signal and can raise heart rate and jitters, which feels like the alarm.

beats.scene: A clock with a coffee cup at noon and a sleepy moon at midnight
beats.summary: Caffeine takes about five to six hours to halve in the body on average, so an afternoon coffee can disturb sleep.

beats.scene: A glass of wine on a bedside table beside a restless, tossing sleeper
beats.summary: Alcohol may feel relaxing at first, but it disturbs sleep and many people feel more anxious the next day.

beats.scene: A cigarette snapped in half beside a clock
beats.summary: Nicotine is a stimulant; smoking seems to calm because it relieves cravings, and a pharmacist or doctor can help anyone who wants to stop.

beats.scene: A plate of simple food and a clock at noon
beats.summary: Skipping meals lets blood sugar dip, which can cause irritability and shakiness; regular meals keep mood and energy steadier.

beats.scene: Ravi eats a simple lunch at a table by a window
beats.summary: Ravi eats lunch at a table instead of at his desk, and slow eating helps the body's rest-and-digest system.

beats.scene: A water bottle on a desk next to a tired face turning cheerful
beats.summary: Even mild dehydration can lower mood and concentration in some studies, so Ravi keeps a water bottle on his desk.

beats.scene: A bowl of ice cream and a tray of fresh fruit on a table
beats.summary: Comfort eating is human and not shameful; sweet foods bring short relief, and no single food, drink or supplement is proven to cure stress.

beats.scene: Ravi ticks a checklist beside a coffee cup, a plate and a bottle
beats.summary: A week of small swaps works: Ravi's body card is done and his diary scores begin to fall.

beats.scene: Meera taps the Mind card on Ravi's desk while he reads a note

Ravi learns two words that are easy to mix up. A stressor is the demand that arrives, and the stress response is what the body and mind do about it.
Stressors come in many kinds, including heat, pain, deadlines and arguments. Even happy events, such as a wedding or a new job, can place demands on the body.
Deep inside the brain, there is a small almond-shaped region called the amygdala. In fact there are two of them, one on each side, and they watch for signs of danger.
Some signals from the eyes and ears seem to reach the amygdala by a quick shortcut. That is why you can jump back from a shape on the path before you know what it is.
Next to the alarm sits a region called the hypothalamus. It works like a control room, because it passes the alarm on to the body's nerves and hormones.
Behind the forehead lies the prefrontal cortex, which does the slower thinking. It can calm a false alarm by deciding that nothing dangerous is happening, but it works less well when we are tired.
At two o'clock that afternoon, a loud bell rings through the whole school. Ravi's heart leaps before he has had any time to think.

Within seconds, Ravi's heart is beating faster and his breathing has become quick and shallow. His palms feel damp, and his mouth has gone dry.
The chemical behind all this is adrenaline, which is a hormone, or a messenger carried in the blood. It is made in two small adrenal glands that sit on top of the kidneys.
Nerves carry the order from the brain to the glands in only seconds. This fast system is called the sympathetic nervous system, and it works like the accelerator of a car.
The heart beats faster and harder, so that it can send more blood to the muscles. The lungs take in more air at the same time, to bring extra oxygen.
The pupils in the eyes open wider and the senses become sharper. Sweating starts too, because it will help to cool a body that may have to work hard.
Adrenaline also tells the liver to release stored sugar, called glucose, into the blood. This gives the muscles and the brain a quick supply of fuel.
Ravi leads Class Seven B safely out into the playground. On the way, one pupil stops and stands completely still, because freezing is also a normal response to alarm.
The head teacher calls the all clear, and everyone relaxes. Ravi's hands are still trembling, because adrenaline takes several minutes to fade from the body.

That evening Meera sends photos of her handwritten notes. They say that adrenaline is the sprinter of the stress response, while cortisol is the long-distance runner.
If the danger lasts for more than a few seconds, the brain uses a second route. A pea-sized pituitary gland passes a message to the adrenal glands.
At the end of that chain, the adrenal glands release cortisol, which is a steroid hormone. It rises over several minutes, and it can take an hour or more to fade again.
Cortisol raises the level of sugar in the blood and helps to keep blood pressure up. In this way it gives the body energy to keep going for longer.
Cortisol has a bad reputation, but it is not an enemy. People whose bodies make too little of it become seriously ill, so everybody needs some.
Cortisol follows a daily rhythm, and it is usually highest soon after you wake up. It then falls slowly through the day and is lowest around midnight.
When there is enough cortisol in the blood, it sends a message back to the brain. The message tells the brain to turn the alarm down, like a thermostat in a house.
Once danger has passed, a second set of nerves takes over and slows the body down. It is called the parasympathetic system, and its main wire is the long vagus nerve.
During an alarm, the body puts less urgent jobs on pause, such as digesting food and repairing small damage. That is why the mouth feels dry and the stomach feels strange.

Too little pressure makes people bored, and too much makes them overwhelmed. For many tasks the best performance comes somewhere in the middle, like the top of a hill.

Running the alarm system day after day uses up energy, so long-lasting stress often brings deep tiredness. Tiredness has many other possible causes, so anyone who feels exhausted for weeks should see a doctor.

The gut has its own network of millions of nerve cells, and it talks to the brain all the time. That is why stress can cause butterflies, nausea, cramps and changes in digestion.

A short burst of stress can boost some parts of the immune system. Long-lasting stress, however, is linked with weaker defences, slower healing of wounds and a higher chance of catching colds.

In some studies, long-lasting stress is linked with higher blood sugar and with more fat stored around the middle of the body. The effects differ widely between people, and habits also play a large part.
The good news is that none of this is instant or fixed. Many of the effects ease when the stress eases, and Ravi feels a wave of relief.
Ravi gets through the evening by breathing slowly between conversations. He walks home at ten o'clock, tired but pleased, and wonders what stress does to his thinking.
On Thursday morning, the day of the inspection, Ravi cannot find his lesson plan anywhere. A moment later he forgets the name of a pupil he has taught since September.
Under stress, attention narrows to the possible threat, like a torch with a thin beam. This is useful in danger, but it makes broad and flexible thinking harder.
Working memory is like a small notepad in the mind, and it only holds a few things at once. When worry fills the notepad, there is less room left for the task in hand.
A part of the brain called the hippocampus helps to form memories. Researchers have linked long periods of high stress hormones with memory trouble, which often improves again when the stress eases.
Under heavy pressure, the planning part of the brain does not work as well. We tend to fall back on old habits, and even simple decisions begin to feel difficult.
Stress can bring irritability, tearfulness, a flat mood and worries that spin round and round. It can feed anxiety and low mood, although these are not exactly the same thing as stress.
In the middle of a lesson, Ravi speaks sharply to Sam over a small mistake. He feels sorry at once, and he apologises to Sam before the end of the lesson.

The World Health Organization describes burnout as a result of long-lasting stress at work that has not been managed. It is marked by exhaustion, a feeling of distance from the job and a drop in effectiveness.
The good news is that thinking can recover over time. Studies suggest that many of the changes seen after long stress ease with rest, better sleep and time.
The inspector is polite, and the lesson goes better than Ravi had feared. At five o'clock he collapses into a chair, and he realises that he has been in alarm mode for months.
On Friday at lunch, Ravi asks Tom how he stayed so relaxed during the inspection. They had the same week and the same inspector, yet they felt very differently.
Researchers say that stress depends partly on how we judge a situation. The same event can feel like an exciting challenge to one person and a frightening threat to another.
In general, stress rises when we feel that the demands on us are greater than the resources we have. Resources can mean time, skills, energy, money and helpful people.
Research shows that having some control over a situation makes stress easier to bear. Ravi writes a list of things in his work that he can actually decide for himself.
Knowing what to expect also makes stress easier to bear. Surprises and unclear plans keep the alarm system ready, so a clear timetable can bring calm.
People who have others to talk to usually cope better with stress. Loneliness, on the other hand, can make it feel heavier and harder to carry.
People differ a great deal in how strongly their alarm reacts. Genes, early life, sleep and health all play a part, and a sensitive alarm is not a weakness or a choice.
The mind can sound the alarm about things that have not happened yet, or replay events from the past. The body reacts to these thoughts almost as if the events were really happening.
The good news is that if thoughts and habits matter, then there are levers to pull. Ravi sees that he can reach them through his body, his mind and the way he lives.
On Friday night, Ravi takes three index cards from a drawer. On them he writes Body, Mind and Life, and he props them against his lamp.
On Saturday morning Ravi sits at his desk with the three cards in front of him. It is the first day of the week that he can plan without a bell.
Meera arrives with a bag of croissants and a warning, which is that there is no magic fix. She tells Ravi that a reset is not a single event but a set of habits.
Meera explains how scientists find out what really works. Researchers compare groups of people and measure the average effect, and a modest effect is not the same as a useless one.

Meera sorts the tools on a napkin by evidence. Exercise, sleep habits and talking therapies have strong support, breathing, mindfulness and nature have modest support, and writing about worries has mixed results.
The aim is not to remove all stress, which would be impossible and unhelpful. It is to let the alarm switch off when the moment has passed, and to lower the usual baseline.
They agree to treat each tool as a small experiment, trying one thing at a time. Ravi will keep what helps and drop what does not, and he knows that his results may differ from other people's.
Ravi starts a simple diary with a score from zero to ten each evening. He adds one line about the day, so that patterns will show up over the coming weeks.

Meera adds a safety note, which is that these tools are meant for ordinary everyday stress. Chest pain, fainting, or sudden breathlessness should always be checked by a doctor, and should never be left to a notebook.
They decide to begin with the Body card, because the body is often the quickest door to calm. It is often easier to slow a breath than to slow a thought.
As evening arrives, Ravi puts the Body card on top of the pile. He writes Day one in his diary and looks forward to Monday, which has not happened in a long time.
Meera points out that breathing is special, because it runs by itself but we can also take control of it. That makes it a handle on a system that is otherwise automatic.
In stress people tend to breathe quickly and high in the chest. Calm breathing is slower and lower, so that the belly rises gently as the lungs fill.
Each time we breathe out, the heart slows down a little, and each time we breathe in it speeds up slightly. A long, slow out-breath is therefore a way to give the brake a gentle push.
Researchers think that slow breathing may stimulate the vagus nerve and help the calming system. The exact way it works is still being studied, so the explanations should be held loosely.
Meera teaches Ravi a very simple pattern of breathing. He breathes in through the nose for four counts and out slowly for six, and then he repeats it.
Another popular pattern is called square breathing, with four equal sides. You breathe in for four, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold again.
Some small studies suggest that slow breathing can lower blood pressure a little and ease anxiety. The effect is modest, and breathing exercises are a helpful tool, not a cure.
A few cautions are needed whenever someone tries breathing exercises. Never force the breath or hold it for long, and stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy or start to tingle.
Meera advises him to practise when he is calm, just like a fire drill. A tool that has been practised in quiet moments is much easier to find in a stressful one.
On Thursday of the next week, Sam knocks a pot of blue paint across a desk. Ravi breathes out slowly, and he feels his heart settle, which is not magic, though it helps.
Meera teaches Ravi a method called progressive muscle relaxation, which was developed about a hundred years ago. The idea is simple, because you tense a muscle first and then let it go.
You start with the feet, tensing the muscles for about five seconds and then releasing them. Then you spend ten to twenty seconds noticing how different they feel.
You move slowly upwards through the calves, thighs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders and face. Each group is tightened and then released, and the whole session takes about fifteen minutes.
Many people do not notice how tense they are until the tension goes. The contrast between tight and loose teaches the body what relaxed really feels like.
Studies suggest that progressive muscle relaxation can ease tension and anxiety to a moderate degree. It takes practice to learn, and it works better for some people than for others.
There is also a very short version for the desk. You drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw, let your teeth part and breathe out slowly.
Gentle stretches, such as slow neck rolls or a chest stretch in a doorway, can ease stiffness. They should never hurt, and Ravi must stop if he feels any pain.
Yoga and tai chi are forms of gentle movement that are linked with slow breathing. Studies suggest benefits for stress and mood that are moderate, and the quality of teaching varies.
Warmth can help tight muscles to relax, whether it comes from a bath, a shower or a heat pad on the neck. The evidence is mostly about comfort, but it costs very little.
At bedtime Ravi tries a slow body scan, moving his attention from his toes to his head. He falls asleep before he reaches his knees, and he decides that this still counts as a success.
Meera tells Ravi that stress prepares the body to move, so moving helps to finish the cycle. That afternoon he leaves school and goes for a brisk walk around the park.
Regular physical activity is linked with lower anxiety and a better mood. People often credit chemicals called endorphins, but scientists are still working out the full story.
Many health bodies advise adults to aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity every week. Any amount is better than none, and even short walks count.
Exercise does not have to mean a gym or special clothes. Taking the stairs, dancing in the kitchen, cycling, gardening and playing with children all count as movement.
On a calm evening Ravi walks at sunset in a steady rhythm, and he counts his steps up to ten. After a few minutes his mind begins to quieten.
Studies link time in green places, such as parks and woods, with lower stress. In some small studies, cortisol levels were lower after a nature walk, though the effect is modest.
One idea is that nature holds our attention gently, without demanding anything. Watching leaves in the wind or water in a stream lets a tired mind rest.
Daylight in the morning helps to set the body clock. A short walk outside after waking can make it easier to feel sleepy at the right time that night.
Too much hard exercise can become another stress on the body, so rest days matter. People should listen to their body, and people with heart conditions should ask a doctor before they start.
Tom hears about Ravi's walks and invites him to a lunchtime walking group. Soon three more colleagues join them for a slow lap of the school field.
After another short night, Ravi looks at his diary and sees a pattern. On days when he slept badly, his stress score the next day was always higher.
Sleep helps the brain to store memories and the body to repair itself. Most adults need about seven to nine hours, though the exact amount differs from person to person.
Studies suggest that after a poor night's sleep, the brain's alarm system reacts more strongly. That is why small problems can feel much bigger when we are tired.
The body clock likes a regular pattern, so a steady wake-up time helps. Ravi decides to get up at about the same time on weekends as on school days.
A wind-down time before bed helps the mind to slow down, with dimmer lights and no work. Ravi puts his marking bag in the cupboard at eight o'clock every evening.
Phones keep the mind busy and awake at night. The evidence about blue light is mixed, but exciting or upsetting content clearly keeps people awake, so Ravi leaves his phone out of the bedroom.
A cool, dark and quiet bedroom helps people to sleep. If you are awake for a long time, it is better to get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
Before bed, Ravi writes a short to-do list for the next day. One small study found that people who did this fell asleep a little faster than those who did not.
If he wakes up in the night, Ravi does not look at the clock. He breathes out slowly, and he reminds himself that one poor night is unpleasant but not a disaster.
If trouble sleeping lasts for weeks, it is wise to see a doctor, because help is available. A talking therapy for insomnia has good evidence, and Ravi's own sleep slowly improves.
Ravi counts up a typical day in his diary. It includes five cups of coffee, a bag of crisps for lunch, and a glass of wine to relax in the evening.
Caffeine is a stimulant that blocks the brain's tiredness signal. It can also speed up the heart and cause jitters, which feel very much like a little alarm.
On average, it takes about five to six hours for the body to clear half of the caffeine from a cup of coffee. This means that an afternoon coffee can still be affecting sleep at night.
Alcohol may feel relaxing at first, but it disturbs sleep, especially in the second half of the night. Many people also feel more anxious the day after drinking.

Nicotine is a stimulant, and smoking seems to calm people mainly because it relieves a craving. A doctor or pharmacist can help anyone who wants to stop, and many people find this easier with support.
When people skip meals, blood sugar can dip, and this can make them shaky, irritable and unable to concentrate. Regular meals help to keep mood and energy steadier.
Ravi decides to eat lunch at a proper table, away from his desk and his screen. Eating slowly helps the body to switch into its rest and digest mode.
In some studies, even mild dehydration lowers mood and concentration. Ravi puts a water bottle on his desk and drinks from it during the day.
Comfort eating is very human, and there is no need to feel ashamed. Sweet food brings short relief, but no single food, drink or supplement has been proven to cure stress.
After a week of small swaps, Ravi looks at his diary. His scores have dropped from seven to five, and he marks the Body card as a good start.
Meera picks up the Mind card and explains that thoughts are not facts. Even so, a gloomy thought can set off the body's alarm system just as a real danger can.
Ravi notices a thought that returns at night, which says I am a terrible teacher. He sees how this thought leads to a heavy feeling and then to a pounding heart.
Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is built on the idea that how we interpret events shapes how we feel. It is one of the best-studied talking therapies, and it helps many people with anxiety.
Meera describes some common thinking traps that many people share. They include imagining the worst, believing that you know what others think, and using the word should all the time.
Meera teaches a three-step habit, which is to catch the thought, check it and change it. To check it, you ask what the evidence is and what you would say to a friend.
The aim is not to force a cheerful thought, which would feel false. A better thought is realistic and kind, such as, this is hard, but I have handled hard weeks before.
Writing about worries or feelings for ten or fifteen minutes helps some people. The evidence is mixed, and it is sensible to stop if the writing makes you feel worse.
Another trick is to set aside a short worry time each day, for example fifteen minutes with a timer. When a worry appears at other times, Ravi writes it down and promises to come back to it.
Meera tells Ravi that some worries are about problems he can act on, and others are only imagined scenarios. For the first kind he can take one small next step, and the second kind he can set aside.
Ravi tries to speak to himself like a kind coach, instead of a harsh critic. Research suggests that kindness towards oneself is linked with lower stress, and it does not make people lazy.
Meera suggests trying mindfulness, and Ravi is not convinced. He thinks it sounds like sitting around and doing nothing, when he has far too much to do.
Mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment on purpose, and without judging it. It does not mean emptying the mind, which is practically impossible.
A simple five-minute practice is to sit and notice the breath. When the mind wanders, as it always does, you notice that it has wandered and gently bring it back.
Eight-week mindfulness courses have been studied a great deal. They show modest benefits for stress, anxiety and low mood, which are similar to those of other methods, and they are not a cure.
Mindfulness is not right for every single person in the world. If it brings up strong distress or difficult memories, it is wise to stop and talk to a doctor or a trained professional.
Mindfulness does not need a cushion, because it can be practised during ordinary things. Ravi pays attention to the warmth of a cup of tea, the water on his hands or his feet on the ground.
Meera shares a grounding exercise for moments of panic or worry. You name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste.
Ravi tries one quiet minute with his class before a lesson, and he asks them to listen to the sounds around them. To his surprise, the children are very good at it.
Meera suggests another small habit, which is to write down three good things from the day. Studies find that it can lift mood a little, though the effect is small.
Meera explains that some stress and some feelings cannot be removed. Fighting them can add strain, and it can help to remember that feelings rise and fall, like waves.
Now it is time for the Life card, which is about lightening the load itself. Ravi starts with the most obvious problem, which is the mountain of marking.
Ravi splits the huge pile into small stacks of ten books and puts a sticky note on each. A big job feels impossible, but a small step feels possible.
Each morning he chooses the three most important tasks for the day. Done is often better than perfect, and a short list is more likely to be finished than a long one.
Ravi draws two circles on a sheet of paper. One holds the things he can control, and the other holds the things he cannot, so his energy goes to the right place.
Tom asks Ravi to run the school book fair, and Ravi says no, kindly. He explains that he cannot do it this term, though he offers to help for an hour next term.
Ravi finds the courage to tell Mrs Hale that his workload is too heavy. She listens carefully and moves one duty to another teacher, which makes a real difference.
Short breaks during the day can stop stress from building up. Every hour or so, Ravi stands at the window for two minutes and looks into the distance.
Ravi decides to stop marking at seven in the evening and to switch off his work emails. Being always available is linked with more stress, so he sets limits.
Constant news and notifications can keep the alarm system primed. Ravi decides to check the news at set times, and puts his phone in a drawer in the evening.

Ravi remembers that some stressors, such as money worries, poor housing or caring for a sick relative, are too big for breathing exercises alone. Tools help us to cope, but practical help and fairer conditions matter as well.
Ravi meets his old friend Dev for coffee on Saturday morning. He hesitates for a moment, and then he tells Dev honestly how he has been feeling.
Studies link good relationships with better coping and better health. A good listener does not have to fix anything, and often just hearing someone out is enough.
It helps to tell a friend what you need, whether that is advice or simply someone to listen. Most friends are glad to be asked, and they feel closer afterwards.
Dev's dog, Biscuit, leaps onto Ravi's lap, and he finds himself laughing out loud. Laughter gives a short break from worry, and stroking a friendly dog is linked with lower stress in some studies.
Calm, slow music can lower the heart rate and ease stress for many people. Singing, alone or with others, can help too, and Ravi makes himself a quiet playlist.
A hobby that absorbs you gives the mind a proper rest from worry. Ravi takes out his old sketchbook and draws a bowl of fruit for the first time in years.
An evening routine of a few simple steps tells the body that the day is over. Ravi tidies his desk, dims the lamp and makes a cup of herbal tea.
Meera explains that resilience does not mean being tough, and that it is built from many small habits and from supportive relationships. It can be learned, and Ravi ticks his weekly habit chart.
After a hard period, the body needs time to recover, and rest is not a weakness. Ravi spends a whole Saturday morning on the sofa with nothing planned, and he does not feel guilty.
A bad Tuesday comes back, and Ravi feels discouraged for an evening. In the diary, his scores have drifted down from eight to five over several weeks, so progress is not a straight line.
Meera says that sometimes self-help tools are not enough. If stress lasts for weeks, harms sleep or work, causes panic or leads to heavy drinking, it is time to see a doctor.
Stress, anxiety, low mood and burnout can overlap and feel alike. Only a trained professional can tell them apart, and nobody needs a label before asking for help.
Ravi books an appointment with his doctor, Dr Reyes. He writes a short list of what he wants to say, so that he does not forget anything in the room.
Dr Reyes listens, asks questions and checks Ravi's blood pressure. Sometimes a doctor also arranges simple tests, to make sure that nothing else is causing the symptoms.

In general, a doctor may talk about options such as counselling, CBT or other talking therapies. Medicines are sometimes used for anxiety or depression, and they should never be started or stopped without asking a doctor.
If you ever think about harming yourself, or feel that you cannot go on, please act at once. Call your local emergency number or a crisis helpline, tell someone you trust, and stay with other people.

To help someone else who seems to be struggling, notice the change, ask kindly and listen without trying to fix everything. Encourage them to seek help, and call the emergency services if they are in danger.
A month later, on Monday morning, Ravi still feels a rush of nerves before the first lesson. This time he breathes out slowly, drops his shoulders and tells himself that the feeling will pass.
On Monday night Ravi lies in bed, and his heart is calm. He thinks over what he will keep, which is slow breathing, a daily walk, a wind-down hour and honest talk.
This book has offered general information about stress, and the science is still growing. It is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor if you are worried about your own health.
C1C2: Ravi, a schoolteacher in his thirties, lay on his back in the dark with one hand pressed against his chest, listening to his heart hammer as though it had somewhere urgent to be. Nothing was wrong that he could see, since the house was quiet, the door was locked and the lamp was off. And yet his body seemed to be shouting a warning that his mind could not translate.

As the clock moved past midnight, Ravi began to tally the week ahead the way other people count sheep, except that his tally only made him more alert. Reports were due, a mountain of marking sat in his bag, parents were coming on Wednesday and an inspector was arriving on Thursday. Each item was manageable alone, but together they formed a weight that he could feel pressing on his ribs.

Giving up on sleep for the moment, Ravi padded into the kitchen, poured himself a glass of water and drank it standing at the window. Behind him on the table sat a leaning tower of exercise books, each one a small promise that he had not yet kept. The refrigerator hummed, a tap dripped somewhere in the dark, and still his pulse refused to slow down at all.

Standing in the pale light of the refrigerator, Ravi realised that this was not simply one bad night. For months there had been headaches, a temper shorter than he liked, a habit of misplacing his keys and a tiredness that sleep never seemed to cure. He had called it being busy, but the word suddenly felt too small for what his body had been trying to tell him.

At one in the morning his phone lit up with a message from Meera, his older sister, who was a nurse and was on a quiet stretch of her night shift. She had a sixth sense about him, and she asked simply whether he was awake and whether everything was all right. He typed that his heart was racing and that he had no idea why, then watched the screen until she replied.

Meera answered kindly and carefully, explaining that a racing heart in the small hours is common among people who are tired and under pressure. She added that she could not diagnose anyone by text message, and that if Ravi was worried about his health he should see a doctor rather than rely on her opinion. Still, she said, a body that has been on alert for a long time often behaves exactly like this.

Then Meera wrote a sentence that Ravi would remember for the rest of the week, which was that his body was not broken but was doing an ancient job a little too well. She promised that once he understood what the job was, the fear that came with it would start to shrink. He stared at the message and felt, for the first time that night, a flicker of curiosity instead of dread.

Rummaging in a drawer, Ravi found a clean notebook that he had been saving for something important, and he wrote a question across the top of the first page. It read, What is my body doing, and what can I do about it? Below it he added three smaller questions, covering the racing heart, the constant tiredness and the possibility that there was a way to switch it all off.

Ravi decided, with the quiet seriousness of a man who teaches for a living, to turn the coming week into a small course of study with himself as the only student. Each day he would ask one question about stress, and he would trust only the answers that had real evidence behind them. It was a plan that cost nothing and asked for very little, which was precisely why he believed he might keep it.

Perhaps it was the plan itself, or perhaps it was simply exhaustion, but at about three in the morning his breathing finally slowed and he drifted off with the notebook open beside him. The alarm would ring in just three hours, and he knew that he would pay for the short night later. Even so, he went to sleep with something he had lacked for months, which was a direction.

Monday arrived far too quickly, and Ravi found himself wedged into a crowded bus with a paper cup of coffee and a bag that weighed as much as a small child. The engine roared, someone's music leaked from their headphones, and he could feel his shoulders creeping steadily towards his ears. It occurred to him that he was about to spend a week studying a thing he was currently feeling.

In the staff room, Tom, who taught mathematics next door and rarely seemed rattled by anything, remarked that Ravi looked as though he had not slept since the summer holidays. Ravi laughed, then surprised them both by asking what stress actually was, beyond a word that everybody used and nobody defined. Tom shrugged and said he had always assumed it meant having too much to do.

That evening Ravi discovered that the word stress began its life in engineering, where it describes the force pressing on a beam, a bridge or a steel cable. A bridge is designed to bend a little under a heavy lorry and spring back afterwards, but if the load never lifts, the metal slowly tires. The image fitted uncomfortably well with how he had been feeling for months, and he copied the picture into his notebook.

Ravi drew two columns in his notebook and learned that people often use one word for two quite different things. The stressor is whatever arrives from outside or inside, such as an exam, a loud noise or a worry, while the stress response is everything the body and mind do in reply. Separating them felt oddly freeing, because it meant the demand and his reaction were two things rather than one.

Stressors turn out to come in every shape, from physical ones like heat, injury or hunger to mental ones like deadlines, and from emotional ones like grief to social ones like a quarrel with a friend. Even happy events, such as a wedding, a new baby or a promotion, ask a great deal of the body and the mind. Nobody, it seemed, lived entirely without them, and nobody would really want to, since a life with no demands would be a very empty one.

Deep inside the brain, on each side, sits a small almond-shaped region called the amygdala, named after the Greek word for an almond. It is part of a network that scans everything the senses report for signs of danger or importance, from a sudden shout to a face that looks angry. Scientists are quick to add that many other regions help, so the amygdala is better described as a key member of the team than as its only player.

Some signals from the eyes and ears appear to reach the amygdala by a quick shortcut, arriving before the slower thinking parts of the brain have finished their analysis. This explains why a person can leap away from a curved shape on the path before realising that it is only a garden hose. Researchers still debate the details of the wiring, but the practical lesson is clear, which is that the body often acts first and asks questions later.

Close to the alarm sits the hypothalamus, a structure no larger than an almond that behaves like a busy control room for the whole body. When the amygdala signals trouble, the hypothalamus translates the message into orders, sending instructions along the nerves and through the chemical messengers of the bloodstream. Within moments a thought has become a bodily event, and nothing has needed to move except a little electricity and a few drops of chemistry.

Behind the forehead lies the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that plans, weighs evidence and decides that the shape on the path really is a hose. It can calm a false alarm and work like a brake, though it is slower than the amygdala and tends to perform badly when a person is exhausted or overwhelmed. This, Ravi realised, was why his own thinking seemed so unreliable at two in the morning.

At two o'clock that afternoon, with Class Seven B halfway through a spelling test, a harsh electric bell began to ring through every corridor of the school. Ravi's heart leapt in his chest before a single thought had formed, which proved, rather neatly, everything that his notebook had said in the morning. His morning's reading on the body's alarm system had just become a live and rather noisy demonstration.

The bell clanged on, and Ravi told Class Seven B in a steady voice to put down their pens and form a line by the door. He sounded calm, which surprised him, because every other part of his body felt as though it were preparing for a race. It was an odd sensation to stand so still on the outside while so much was happening within.

Within seconds, Ravi's heart was beating faster and harder, his breathing had turned quick and shallow, and his palms were damp against the register he was holding. His mouth had gone dry, his skin felt prickly and every sound in the corridor seemed sharper than usual. None of this was a decision, for it was simply a sequence that had been set in motion the moment the bell began.

The chemical behind this sudden transformation is adrenaline, a hormone, which is a messenger substance released into the blood to carry instructions around the body. It is made by the two adrenal glands, each about the size of a walnut, that sit like little caps on top of the kidneys. Within seconds of the alarm, nerves tell these glands to release a surge of adrenaline.

The order travels along nerves rather than through the blood, which is why it arrives so quickly, within a few seconds of the first alarm. This fast network is called the sympathetic nervous system, and the simplest way to picture it is as the accelerator pedal of a car. When it is pressed, the whole body moves from idling to readiness almost instantly.

The heart beats faster and more forcefully, pushing blood towards the large muscles that might be needed for running or fighting, while the lungs draw in air more quickly to supply extra oxygen. The skin may turn pale as blood is redirected away from the surface, and this is partly why a frightened face can look drained of colour. Every adjustment is small, but together they turn the body into a machine ready for action.

The pupils open wider to let in more light, the senses sharpen and a person becomes startlingly aware of small details such as a distant door slamming. Sweat appears on the palms and forehead, which makes sense because a body about to work hard will soon need cooling. Even the strange fluttering in the stomach belongs to this same sequence, as blood is steered away from digestion.

Adrenaline also instructs the liver to release some of its stored sugar, known as glucose, into the bloodstream, where it becomes a fast supply of fuel for the muscles and the brain. The body, in other words, does not wait for lunch when it believes that energy may be needed urgently. It simply opens its own pantry, which is a remarkably efficient arrangement for emergencies and a rather wasteful one for spelling tests.

Ravi led the class down the stairs and out into the playground, speaking in short, clear sentences, and thought how useful his racing pulse had been in keeping him alert. On the way, one pupil stopped dead and could not move, and Ravi gently took the child's hand, remembering that freezing is another natural reaction to alarm. People talk about fight or flight, but the body, it appears, sometimes chooses neither and simply holds still.

When Mrs Hale announced that the drill was over, a ripple of relief ran through the playground, and the teachers began to joke with one another. Ravi's hands, however, continued to tremble for several minutes, because adrenaline fades only gradually once it has been released. The alarm had stopped, but the body needed a little time to hear the news.

Back in the classroom, a boy named Sam, who asked questions the way other children breathe, wanted to know why Mr Ravi's hands were shaking. Ravi explained, in simple words, that his body had been getting ready to help the whole class, and that the shaking was its way of finishing the job. Watching Sam nod, Ravi understood that he was learning faster by explaining than he had ever done by reading.

That evening Meera sent photographs of her handwritten notes, which she had written in neat capital letters during a quiet hour on the ward. Her main idea was a comparison, in which adrenaline was the sprinter that bursts away at the sound of the gun and cortisol was the long-distance runner that keeps going. Ravi laughed, because it was the first explanation of hormones that he had ever been able to picture.

If the danger lasts longer than a few seconds, the brain switches to a second and slower route that runs through a chain of three small organs. The hypothalamus sends a chemical message to the pituitary gland, a structure about the size of a pea at the base of the brain, and the pituitary in turn sends a message to the adrenal glands. Scientists use a long name for this chain, but Ravi simply called it the slow line.

At the end of the slow line the adrenal glands release cortisol, a steroid hormone that rises over several minutes, reaches a peak after perhaps half an hour and can take an hour or more to fade. Adrenaline is gone almost before you notice, but cortisol lingers like the smell of toast after the toaster has been switched off. This delay is why a person can still feel jumpy long after a fright is over.

Cortisol raises the level of sugar in the blood, helps to keep blood pressure steady and, for a short time, calms down inflammation, which is the body's own swelling and heat. All of this gives the body what it needs to keep going through a difficult stretch, whether that is a long journey, an illness or a hard day's work. Seen this way, cortisol is less a villain than a rather dependable emergency supplier.

Cortisol has acquired a bad reputation in magazines, where it is often called the stress hormone as if it were a poison, but that picture is badly incomplete. People whose bodies make too little of it become seriously ill, and everyone needs a healthy supply every single day just to stay alive. The problems appear only when the level stays too high for too long, or when its natural daily rhythm is lost.

Even without any stress, cortisol rises and falls in a daily rhythm, climbing in the early hours of the morning so that the body is ready to get going. It is highest soon after waking, falls gradually through the afternoon and reaches its lowest point at about midnight. For Ravi this was a small revelation, since it suggested that the alarm in his chest at midnight was fighting against the calm that his body was trying to produce.

The system includes a built-in safeguard, because when there is enough cortisol in the blood it sends a message back to the brain asking for the alarm to be turned down. Engineers call this a feedback loop, and it works like the thermostat in a house, which switches the heating off once the room is warm. When the loop works well the response is brief, and when it is overwhelmed the heating simply keeps running.

Once the danger has passed, a second set of nerves, the parasympathetic system, takes over and does the opposite of what adrenaline did. If the sympathetic system is the accelerator, this one is the brake, slowing the heart and encouraging digestion and rest. Its principal cable is the long, wandering vagus nerve, which runs from the brainstem down to the heart, the lungs and the gut.

During an alarm the body pushes less urgent jobs to the bottom of its list, including digestion, growth, repair and the making of some reproductive hormones. This explains why the mouth turns dry, why the stomach flutters and why people rarely feel hungry in the middle of a frightening moment. In a short emergency that postponement costs almost nothing, but over many weeks it begins to look like neglect.

Before bed Ravi drew a simple chart in his notebook, with adrenaline in one column marked seconds and cortisol in the other marked minutes to hours. Beneath it he wrote the central lesson of the day, which was that both chemicals are useful and both are meant to switch off once the danger is over. Then he added the question that had been circling in his mind, which was what happens to a person whose alarm never stops.

On Tuesday morning Ravi had to give a five-minute talk in front of the entire school, an event that would normally have filled him with dread. His heart was thumping and his mouth was dry, yet he noticed with interest that his mind felt unusually clear and his words came readily. Somewhere between the first sentence and the last, he understood that this stress was working in his favour.

A short burst of stress can sharpen the senses, speed up reactions and flood the body with useful energy. Athletes know this well, which is why many of them feel nervous before a race and some become suspicious if the nerves fail to arrive. Used in this way, the stress response is a kind of natural coaching system that raises performance at exactly the moment it is needed.

Good stress even has a name of its own, eustress, which borrows the Greek prefix for good. It is the pleasant tension of a challenge that excites you instead of crushing you, such as learning a new skill, playing a close game or walking into a first date. The body's chemistry is similar to that of bad stress, but the feeling attached to it is of energy and hope instead of dread.

Psychologists have long described the link between pressure and performance as an upside-down U, with boredom on the left, overload on the right and the best results somewhere near the top. The idea is more than a century old and the details are still argued over, since the peak sits in a different place for different people and for different tasks. Even so, Ravi found it a helpful picture, and he drew it on the board for Sam.

Ravi compared two pages of his diary, one from a week when he had been busy but in control, and one from a recent week that had been stuffed with deadlines. On the first page the day had a rhythm, with effort followed by rest, while on the second there was no gap anywhere, only a wall of tasks. He had been living far beyond the top of the curve for longer than he cared to admit.

The size of a single event is rarely the real problem, for the body copes well with a sharp shock followed by rest. Trouble comes when stress continues for weeks or months with no chance to recover, a state doctors call chronic stress, from a Greek word for time. What matters, then, is not only how high the alarm rings but how long it is allowed to go on ringing.

Modern life is rich in stressors that last, among them endless emails, constant notifications, noise, crowded journeys, money worries and the feeling of being permanently reachable. Most of these cannot be escaped by running away or defeated by a quick fight, so the energy that the body prepares has nowhere to go. It simply stays inside the person, who is usually sitting at a desk and doing nothing about it.

The alarm system evolved long before anyone had invented the email, yet it often responds to a hostile message as if it were a threat to life. The machinery that answers a growling dog is largely the same machinery that answers an angry parent or a looming deadline, though the details differ. Our thoughts and our worries can pull the same lever, and the body obeys without checking whether any teeth are involved.

A system designed for short sprints is being asked to run a marathon without a rest, and the strain accumulates silently. Like a car engine left revving in the driveway all day, it burns fuel, heats up and wears its parts without going anywhere at all. Researchers describe this accumulated cost as wear and tear, and it is the reason why recovery cannot be treated as a luxury.

On Tuesday night Ravi wrote a new line in his notebook and underlined it twice, which said that recovery is part of the job and not a reward for finishing it. He had always treated rest as something to be earned after the work was done, and the work was never done. Closing the notebook, he wondered what that long habit had been doing to his own body.

On Wednesday morning Ravi had slept for barely five hours, and he sat at the breakfast table feeling as though someone had filled his head with wet sand. Even buttering the toast seemed to require a decision, and the day ahead looked like a long uphill road. He opened the notebook with a sigh, because today's question was about what long stress does to the body.

Meera's notes listed the common signs of long-lasting stress, among them poor sleep, tiredness, headaches, aches, restlessness and a temper that flares more easily than usual. People frequently notice these changes in themselves long before they connect them with pressure, and they blame the weather, their age or their mattress instead. Ravi ticked off more of the list than he wished to admit, and he did so in pencil, as though that might make it less true.
