Under stress, muscles tighten in readiness for action, and the neck, shoulders and jaw are among the first to respond. This is helpful for a sprint but not for marking essays, since the tension has no movement to release it and so it just sits there, drawing the body into a defensive curl. Halfway through a lesson, Ravi caught his own shoulders hovering near his ears and his teeth clamped together.

A tension headache often feels like a band tightening around the head, and it is linked with tense muscles in the neck, jaw and scalp. These headaches are very common and usually harmless, although a sudden, severe or unusual headache is a reason to seek medical advice without delay. Ravi noticed that his own appeared most often on the afternoons when he had skipped lunch and sat hunched over the marking.

A common misunderstanding is that pain linked with stress is somehow imaginary, but that is false, because the aching is real and the muscles are truly tight. A nervous system that is constantly on alert can turn up the volume on pain signals, so that ordinary neck and back aches feel stronger and last longer. This works in both directions, since pain itself is stressful and so feeds the very cycle that makes it worse.

A body that is on high alert finds it hard to power down at night, which creates the odd and familiar condition of being exhausted yet unable to sleep. People often wake at three in the morning with a busy mind, and the poor night then makes the following day feel harder, which adds to the stress. Sleep and stress, in other words, are locked in a loop that can turn in either direction.

Keeping the alarm system running day after day consumes energy, and poor sleep removes the chance to refill the tank, so deep tiredness is a typical companion of long-lasting stress. Fatigue, however, has a great many other possible causes, some of them medical, and nobody should assume that stress explains it. Anyone who feels exhausted for weeks should therefore talk to a doctor instead of guessing.

Stress alters behaviour as well as chemistry, and the two changes tend to reinforce one another. Some people eat more when they are under pressure while others lose their appetite, and many drink extra coffee, scroll through their phones late at night and drop the exercise that once helped them. Ravi recognised the pattern with a wince, since his own week had included three biscuits for breakfast.

For some people the skin becomes a visible diary of stressful periods, with eczema, acne or other conditions flaring up when life becomes difficult. The link is real for many but not for all, and stress is rarely the only cause, because genes, weather, products and many other factors also play a part. Anyone troubled by a skin problem can ask a doctor or a pharmacist about it.

At lunchtime Meera phoned Ravi and reminded him, firmly and kindly, that none of these signs proves anything on its own, because each of them can have many causes. She suggested that he keep a short diary, not as a way of diagnosing himself but as a way of noticing patterns over time. He wrote the heading, Notice, do not diagnose, and felt strangely relieved to have a rule.

Before the first parent arrived on Wednesday evening, Ravi could feel his heart knocking against his ribs, and he pressed two fingers to his wrist to measure it. His pulse was racing, which struck him as both reassuring and absurd, for it simply meant that his body was treating a pleasant conversation about spelling as an emergency. He took a slow breath and decided to treat the moment as a laboratory.

During stress the heart beats faster and blood pressure climbs, and for a short time this is entirely normal and even healthy, because the muscles need fuel and the brain needs oxygen. The body expects each rise to be followed by a fall, as a swing rises and then returns to its resting position. A healthy cardiovascular system is one that can do both, and can do them quickly and smoothly without any lasting strain.

When the surges happen again and again for years, researchers find links with a higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease, partly through the body's own responses and partly through habits like smoking and poor sleep. Stress is only one of many factors, however, and the evidence shows a connection rather than a simple cause. It is a reason to take stress seriously, not a reason to be frightened.

High blood pressure usually announces itself with no symptoms at all, which is why people can live with it for years without knowing. Fortunately it is quick and painless to measure, and a doctor, nurse or pharmacist can check it and explain what the numbers mean for an individual person. Ravi, who had not had his checked in years, wrote a note to book an appointment.

The gut contains its own network of millions of nerve cells, which is sometimes nicknamed the second brain, and it talks to the real brain constantly along the vagus nerve and through chemical messages. This is why anxiety can produce butterflies, nausea, cramps, an urgent need for the toilet or no appetite whatsoever. The stomach, it turns out, is a surprisingly emotional organ, and it often reacts before the mind has noticed anything at all.

Stress can make some digestive conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, flare up or feel worse, although it is not usually their only cause. That does not mean that the symptoms are imaginary or are all in the mind, because the discomfort is perfectly real and has real biological roots. A person with lasting stomach trouble should see a doctor, who can check that nothing else is going on.

A short burst of stress can briefly boost parts of the immune system, which makes sense for a body that expects an injury. Long-lasting stress, however, is linked with weaker defences, slower healing of wounds and, in some studies, a greater chance of developing a cold after contact with a virus. The effects are modest and vary a great deal, but they offer one more reason to treat rest as a serious health habit.

In some studies, long-lasting stress is linked with higher blood sugar and with fat being stored around the waist, and cortisol is thought to play a part in both. The effects differ widely from person to person, and habits such as eating, sleeping and moving also play a very large role. Nobody should blame themselves for their weight or their body shape on the basis of a few hormones.

The best news in Meera's notes was that none of this happens overnight and none of it is fixed forever. The body is a patient repair shop, and many of the effects of stress ease when the stress eases, as the thermostat begins to work again and the daily rhythm returns. Ravi leaned back in his chair and felt a wave of relief wash over him, which, he noticed, was itself a calming chemical event.

Ravi survived the evening by letting out a slow breath between each conversation, and the parents, who were kind and mostly anxious themselves, seemed not to notice anything unusual. He walked home at ten o'clock under the street lights, tired but oddly pleased, and a text from Meera suggested that tomorrow he should think about his mind. He agreed, though he suspected that his own mind would turn out to be the harder and more stubborn subject.

On Thursday morning, the day of the inspection, Ravi turned his desk upside down looking for a lesson plan that was lying under his elbow. A few minutes later he blanked on the name of a pupil he had taught every day since September, and he felt a flush of embarrassment. It was a small lapse, but it made him wonder what his mind had been doing lately.

Under stress, attention contracts around the possible threat like the beam of a narrow torch, which is exactly what a person needs when something dangerous is approaching. The price is that everything outside the beam, including the quiet details and the bigger picture, drops out of sight. It is the reason why people under pressure can overlook obvious solutions that are sitting just beyond the light.

Working memory acts like a small notepad in the mind, a limited space where we hold a phone number, a sentence or the next step of a plan. When worry scribbles all over that notepad, less space remains for the task in hand, so that people who are anxious often find simple things strangely difficult. It is not that they are less intelligent, only that part of their mind is busy elsewhere.

A region of the brain called the hippocampus, shaped a little like a seahorse, plays a central role in forming and recalling memories. Researchers have linked long periods of high stress hormones with trouble in this area, and with forgetfulness in everyday life, although the findings are complex and the effects are often reversible. Ravi was comforted to learn that his lost keys might have a biological explanation.

Under heavy pressure, the planning region at the front of the brain works less efficiently, as though a dimmer switch had been turned down, while the alarm region grows louder. People tend to fall back on old habits and quick reactions, and even simple decisions, such as what to cook for dinner, start to feel exhausting. This is the real explanation for the tired shrug of someone who says that they just cannot decide.

Stress can bring irritability, tearfulness, a flat and joyless mood and worries that spin around the mind like washing in a machine. It can feed into anxiety and depression, which are separate conditions with their own features, and which sometimes need professional help. A person who cannot tell which is which does not need to solve the puzzle alone, because a doctor is trained to do exactly that.

In the middle of the lesson, Sam spilled a pot of pencils across the floor, and Ravi heard himself speak far more sharply than the incident deserved. The regret arrived almost before the words had finished, and a minute later he knelt beside the boy, helped to gather the pencils and apologised. Sam, with the generous good humour of eleven-year-olds, simply said that everyone has bad days and that even his dog had several.

The World Health Organization describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon, meaning a condition that arises from long-lasting stress at work that has not been successfully managed. It is marked by three features, namely deep exhaustion, a growing sense of distance or cynicism towards the job, and a fall in effectiveness. Ravi saw with a pang that the second feature had crept into his own thoughts without announcing itself.

The encouraging news was that the thinking brain is remarkably adaptable, and studies suggest that many of the changes seen after long stress ease again with rest, better sleep and time. Nothing in the research promised that this would be quick or complete for everyone. Even so, the direction of travel was hopeful, and Ravi felt that a door had been opened that he had assumed was shut.

The inspector turned out to be polite, the lesson went better than Ravi had dared hope, and by the end of the afternoon the whole ordeal was over. At five o'clock he sank into a chair in the empty classroom, and the weariness that rolled over him was the weariness of someone who had been in alarm mode for months. It was not the inspection that had exhausted him but the long habit of bracing for it.

On Friday at lunch, Ravi asked Tom how he had managed to stay so relaxed throughout the inspection, since they had faced the same week, the same inspector and the same pile of paperwork. Tom thought about it seriously for a while and replied that he honestly did not know the answer himself. That unanswered question became the subject of Ravi's last lesson of the week, and it would shape everything that followed.

Researchers have found that stress depends partly on how a situation is judged, which means that the same event can feel like an exciting challenge to one person and a frightening threat to another. A challenge says that this is hard but I can try, while a threat says that this is too much and I will fail. The body listens carefully to which of the two stories the mind is telling.

In general, stress tends to climb when a person feels that the demands placed on them are greater than the resources they can call upon. Resources include time, skill and energy, but also money, information and helpful people, and they can often be increased even when the demands cannot be reduced. This was an encouraging idea, because it turned a hopeless pile of tasks into a problem with two sides to adjust.

Research in workplaces and laboratories has repeatedly found that having some control over a situation makes it easier to bear, even when the control is quite small. Ravi took a sheet of paper and listed the things in his working week that he could in fact decide for himself, and to his surprise the list ran to eleven items. He had been feeling like a passenger, and it turned out that he was holding several of the controls.

Predictability matters almost as much as control, because a person who knows what is coming can prepare, while a person who does not must stay on guard all the time. Surprises, unclear plans and constantly changing demands keep the alarm system primed, and this may be why Ravi had felt more tired during the vague weeks than during the busy but clear ones. A clear timetable, he decided, was a kind of anti-stress device that cost nothing and could be pinned to any wall.

People who have others to lean on usually cope better with pressure, and studies link good relationships with better health and longer lives, though they do not prove that friendship alone is the cause. Loneliness, by contrast, tends to make stress feel heavier, because the burden has no one to share it. Ravi realised that he had not had a proper conversation with a friend in nearly two months.

People differ in how strongly their alarm system reacts, and the differences come from a mixture of genes, early experience, current health, sleep and circumstances. A sensitive system is not a sign of weakness or a failure of character, any more than being tall or short is a matter of effort. It simply means that some people need to be more careful with their recovery, and Ravi suspected that he was one of them.

Unlike most animals, human beings can sound the alarm over events that have not happened yet, or replay unpleasant events from the past again and again. This looping habit is called rumination when it concerns the past and worry when it concerns the future, and the body reacts to such thoughts almost as strongly as it does to real events. Ravi thought of his sleepless Sunday, when a meeting that had not yet taken place had already made his heart race.

The encouraging consequence of all this research was that, if thoughts, habits and circumstances shape the stress response, then there are levers that a person can actually pull. Ravi sketched them in his notebook and saw that they fell naturally into three groups, one that worked through the body, one that worked through the mind and one that worked through the way he lived. It was not a cure, but it was a map, and he had not had a map before.

On Friday night, as the first week of his experiment came to a close, Ravi took three index cards from a drawer and wrote one word on each of them. They said Body, Mind and Life, and he propped them against his lamp where he would see them every evening. He felt the quiet satisfaction of a person who has finished the theory and is about to begin the practice.

Saturday morning arrived without a bell, a timetable or a single parent waiting in the corridor, and Ravi sat at his desk with the three cards fanned out in front of him. For the first time in months he had the leisure to plan rather than merely react. It felt faintly unnatural, rather like walking on a floor that did not move.

Meera arrived mid-morning with a paper bag of croissants and a warning that she delivered before even taking off her coat. There was, she said, no magic fix, and anyone who claimed otherwise was probably selling something. A reset was not a single event but a set of habits, and the real work would begin on Monday and carry on for weeks.

Meera explained how scientists decide what works, which is by comparing groups of people who try a method with groups who do not and then measuring the average difference. A modest effect on average can still be meaningful for an individual, in the same way that a small tilt in the road can still decide where a very long journey ends. She asked him to hold both thoughts, namely that nothing here was magic and that nothing here was pointless.

She sorted the tools on a napkin according to the strength of the evidence, which was a habit she had picked up on the wards. Exercise, healthy sleep habits and cognitive behavioural therapy stood on the strongest ground, breathing exercises, mindfulness and time in nature on modest ground, and writing about worries on ground that was still mixed. The napkin looked scruffy but it was the most honest document Ravi had ever been given.

The aim, Meera stressed, was not to eliminate stress, which would be both impossible and undesirable, but to let the alarm switch off properly once a moment had passed. A second aim was to lower the baseline, so that the body began each day from a calmer level and had more room to spare for the demands that came. Ravi wrote this down at the top of the Body card, and underlined the word baseline.

They agreed to treat each tool as a small experiment, to be tried one at a time for long enough to learn something about it. What helped would be kept, what did not would be dropped without guilt, and nobody would pretend that his results had to match anyone else's. It was an approach that suited a teacher, since it turned self-improvement into a piece of homework that he was actually allowed to mark himself.

Ravi designed a simple diary in which each evening he would give the day a stress score from zero to ten and add a single line about what had happened. The purpose was not to prove anything dramatic but to let patterns emerge slowly over the coming weeks, as faint trails appear across a field. He wrote the first entry at once, which was a seven, with the note, Saturday, planning, quiet.

Before she left, Meera added a safety note, which she delivered with the seriousness of a person who had seen what happens when people wait. These tools were meant for ordinary, everyday stress, and symptoms such as chest pain, fainting or sudden breathlessness needed to be checked by a doctor rather than put down to nerves. Ravi wrote this on the back of the Body card, and underlined it, so that he would never forget it.

They decided to begin with the Body card, partly because the physical tools are concrete and partly because the body is often the quickest door to calm. It is frequently easier to slow a breath, loosen a shoulder or take a walk than to argue a worry out of existence at midnight. Meera pointed out that the two directions work together, since a calmer body makes calmer thinking more likely.

As the evening light turned the window gold, Ravi placed the Body card on top of the pile and wrote the words Day one in his diary. He noticed, with some astonishment, that he was looking forward to Monday, which was a feeling that he had not had for as long as he could remember. The thought was small and entirely welcome, and it kept him company through a quiet Saturday night.

Meera pointed out that breathing occupies a unique position among the body's automatic functions, since it runs by itself all day yet can also be taken under conscious control. We cannot decide to slow the heart or to calm the stomach, but we can decide to breathe slowly. It is, she said, the one handle that the body offers on a system that otherwise ignores our instructions.

Under stress people tend to breathe quickly and shallowly, high up in the chest, in a pattern that matches the body's readiness to run. Calm breathing is slower and lower, so that the belly rises gently as the diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs, pulls downward. Ravi laid one hand on his stomach and was startled to discover that it had not moved all day.

Each time we breathe in, the heart speeds up very slightly, and each time we breathe out it slows down again, a natural pattern that doctors can measure on a monitor. A long, slow out-breath therefore gives the calming system a gentle push, rather like touching the brake pedal of a car. The effect on any single breath is tiny, but repeated for a few minutes it can be surprisingly noticeable.

Researchers believe that slow breathing may activate the vagus nerve and strengthen the calming side of the nervous system, which would explain why it so often brings a sense of ease. The precise mechanism is still being studied, however, and any neat explanation should be held loosely, since science tends to complicate the stories that we tell about it. What can be said with confidence is that the technique is simple, cheap and safe for most people.

Meera taught him a simple pattern, in which he breathed in quietly through the nose for a count of four and then out slowly for a count of six, with the lips slightly parted. The exact numbers mattered less than the principle, which was that the out-breath should be longer than the in-breath and entirely unforced. After about five minutes, Ravi noticed that the knot beneath his breastbone had loosened a little.

Another popular pattern is known as square or box breathing, in which a person breathes in for a count of four, holds for four, breathes out for four and pauses for four more. Many people enjoy it because the equal sides give the mind something orderly to follow, almost like a tiny piece of music. Ravi preferred the longer out-breath, but he agreed that the best pattern is the one a person will actually use.

Some small studies suggest that regular slow breathing can lower blood pressure slightly and ease feelings of anxiety, although many of these studies are short and the results vary. The honest summary is that the effect is real but modest, and that breathing exercises are a handy everyday tool rather than a cure for anything. Meera made him say this sentence out loud, so that he would not oversell it to himself.

A few cautions are needed, Meera said, because breathing exercises are gentle but not entirely without limits. A person should never force the breath or hold it for long, and should stop if they feel dizzy or start to tingle, while anyone with a lung or heart condition or a pregnancy should ask a doctor first. Ravi copied the warning onto the back of his card, next to her earlier safety note.

Meera advised him to practise when he was calm, in the way that a school rehearses its fire drill on an ordinary Tuesday, so that the routine is familiar when the real bell rings. A tool that has been used in a quiet moment is far easier to find in a stormy one. Ravi began to practise at the bus stop, in the staff room and for two minutes before he got out of bed.

A few days later Sam knocked a full pot of blue paint across two desks and a pile of drawings, and Ravi felt the familiar surge rise through his chest. He breathed out slowly, counted to six and felt the surge crest and subside, and his voice, when it came, was kind rather than sharp. It was not magic, as Meera had warned, but it was the first time in months that he had felt that he, and not the alarm, was in charge.

Meera taught him a method called progressive muscle relaxation, which a doctor developed about a hundred years ago and which hospitals still use today. The idea is disarmingly simple, since you tense a group of muscles deliberately and then let them go, one group after another. It sounded to Ravi like an exercise for a toddler, but he was willing to be surprised.

You begin with the feet, curling the toes and tightening the muscles firmly, though never painfully, for about five seconds. Then you let go all at once and spend the next ten to twenty seconds noticing how different the muscles feel. Ravi was startled by how heavy and warm his feet seemed afterwards, as if they had been quietly holding their breath.

From the feet you move slowly upwards through the calves, thighs, stomach, hands, arms, shoulders and finally the face, tightening and releasing each group in turn. A full session takes about fifteen minutes, and the rhythm of tension and release has a lulling effect, a little like a tide that goes in and out. By the time he reached his forehead, Ravi realised that his thoughts had stopped racing.

Many people do not notice how tense they are until the tension releases, because a constant background hum becomes invisible. The contrast between tight and loose teaches the body what relaxed really feels like, and that memory can then be summoned at will in a stressful moment. It was a little like noticing a refrigerator that has been humming for hours, which only becomes obvious the instant it stops.

Studies suggest that progressive muscle relaxation can ease tension and anxiety to a moderate degree, and it has been tested in many settings from hospitals to classrooms. It takes practice to learn and works better for some people than for others, so a first attempt that feels clumsy is entirely normal. Meera advised him to try it daily for two weeks before deciding whether it was for him.

There is also a short version that can be done at a desk or in a queue, and nobody around will notice. You drop your shoulders away from your ears, unclench your jaw so that the teeth are slightly apart, let your tongue rest and breathe out slowly. Ravi set a quiet reminder on his phone for the middle of each lesson, and was astonished to find his shoulders up near his ears each time.

Gentle stretches, such as slow neck rolls, shoulder circles or a chest stretch with the arms against a doorframe, can ease the stiffness that comes with a hunched posture. They should feel like a pleasant pull and never like pain, and anyone with an injury or a persistent problem should ask a doctor or a physiotherapist for advice. Ravi added a minute of stretching before the register each morning, and the children, who thought it very funny, soon joined in.

Yoga and tai chi combine gentle movement with slow breathing and attention to the body, and studies suggest that they bring moderate benefits for stress, mood and sleep. The quality of the research varies and so does the quality of classes, so it is worth choosing a qualified teacher and telling them about any injury or health condition. Ravi found a friendly beginner class on Tuesday evenings, and he was by far the stiffest person in the room.

Warmth helps tight muscles to loosen, whether it comes from a hot shower, a bath or a heat pad resting against the neck. The scientific evidence here is mostly about comfort and not about dramatic effects, but a remedy that costs almost nothing and feels pleasant has a lot to recommend it. Ravi took a long bath on Sunday evening, and the knot beneath his shoulder blade finally gave in.

At bedtime Ravi tried a slow body scan, moving his attention gradually from his toes to the top of his head and letting each part grow heavy as it was noticed. He fell asleep somewhere around the knees, which Meera, when he told her, declared to be the best possible outcome and a sign that the exercise had done its job. It was an amusing result for a man who had been awake until three o'clock only a week before.

Meera told Ravi that the stress response prepares the body to move, and that moving is therefore the natural way to complete the cycle that the alarm has started. That afternoon, instead of sinking onto the sofa, he left school and set off on a brisk walk around the park. By the second lap, the tightness across his shoulders had begun to dissolve like sugar in warm tea.

Regular physical activity is linked with lower anxiety, a better mood and better sleep, and the evidence for this is among the strongest in the whole field. People often credit chemicals called endorphins for the post-exercise glow, but scientists are still working out the full story, and several other changes in the brain and body probably contribute. Ravi was content to enjoy the effect for now without needing to understand every detail of how it worked.

Many health organisations advise adults to aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity every week, which sounds a great deal until it is divided into a half-hour walk on five days. Any amount is better than none, and short bursts of ten minutes add up, so the target should be treated as a direction of travel and not a test to be failed. Ravi began with ten minutes a day, which he could not honestly describe as difficult.

Exercise does not have to mean a gym, a lycra suit or a miserable run in the rain, since any activity that raises the heart rate a little and is enjoyable will serve the purpose. Taking the stairs, dancing around the kitchen, cycling to the shops, gardening or playing football with children all count as movement. Ravi found that the best exercise was the kind that did not feel like exercise at all.

On a mild evening he walked at sunset in a steady, unhurried rhythm, counting his steps up to ten and then starting again, a trick that Meera had said could occupy the restless part of the mind. After several minutes the commentary in his head grew quieter and the colours of the sky became more interesting than his to-do list. It was a simple pleasure, and he suspected that it was also a useful one.

Studies link time spent in green places, such as parks, gardens and woods, with lower stress and a better mood, and some small studies have found lower cortisol levels after a walk in nature. The effects are modest and vary from study to study, but they are consistent enough that city planners now pay attention to them. Ravi sat for ten minutes on a park bench and listened to the birds, feeling slightly foolish and entirely content.

One idea, called attention restoration, is that nature holds our attention gently without demanding anything in return, unlike an email or an advertisement that grabs the mind and refuses to let go. Watching leaves stir in the wind or water slide over stones lets the tired focusing system rest and recover. Scientists continue to test the idea, but Ravi simply noticed that he felt more rested after fifteen minutes in the park than after fifteen minutes on his phone.

Daylight in the morning helps to set the body's internal clock, and a short walk outside soon after waking can make it easier to feel sleepy at the right time that night. Even on a cloudy day, outdoor light is far brighter than indoor lighting, which is why a few minutes outside count for more than hours beside a lamp. Ravi began to walk the last stretch to school, and his sleep, to his delight, began to improve.

Meera added a caution, which was that too much hard exercise becomes yet another stress on the body, so rest days matter just as training days do. People should listen to their bodies and stop if they feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest pain, and anyone with a heart condition or other health concern should ask a doctor before beginning a new programme. Ravi, who was more likely to do too little than too much, wrote the caution down anyway.

Tom heard about the walks and invited Ravi to join a lunchtime walking group that he had started with a colleague from the science department. Within a week there were four of them, strolling slowly around the school field, and the conversation was a welcome blend of gossip, jokes and fresh air. It struck Ravi that the group was quietly delivering three of his cards at once, since it offered movement, daylight and company.

After another short night, Ravi opened his diary and noticed a pattern that had been invisible to him before. On the days that followed a poor night, his stress score was always higher, and on the days that followed a decent night it was nearly always lower. The data was crude, but the message was plain, which was that sleep and stress were tied together in both directions.

During sleep the brain files away the day's memories, the body repairs and rebuilds, and the emotional centres appear to reset themselves for the next day. Most adults are advised to aim for about seven to nine hours, although the exact need differs between people and shifts across a lifetime. Ravi, who had been surviving on five or six, realised that he had mistaken endurance for health.

Studies suggest that after a poor night's sleep the brain's alarm system reacts more strongly to upsetting things, while the thinking region that usually calms it responds less effectively. This is one reason why small problems loom so large when we are tired, and why a spilled cup of tea can feel like a catastrophe. Ravi recognised this effect immediately, and he remembered the pot of blue paint with a kind of grim amusement.

The body's internal clock, which scientists call the circadian rhythm, thrives on regularity, and the single most helpful anchor is a steady wake-up time. Ravi decided to rise at about the same hour on Saturdays and Sundays as on school days, which meant sacrificing the long weekend lie-in that he had always thought of as his reward. The first Saturday was painful, the second was merely tolerable and the third was perfectly pleasant.

A wind-down hour before bed gives the mind a chance to shift gradually from the busy day to the quiet night, ideally with softer lights, no work and nothing too stimulating. Ravi began by putting his marking bag in a cupboard at eight o'clock, out of sight and therefore, to a surprising degree, out of mind. He read a paperback instead, and was startled to discover how much he enjoyed novels when he was not too tired to follow the plot.

Phones keep the mind busy and the alarm system alert, and the scientific evidence about the effect of blue light on sleep is mixed. What is clear is that exciting, upsetting or endlessly scrolling content keeps people awake, so Ravi began charging his phone in the kitchen overnight. He bought a cheap alarm clock for four pounds, and the arrangement felt like a small declaration of independence.

A cool, dark and quiet bedroom supports sleep, and so does reserving the bed for sleeping rather than for working, worrying or watching films. If a person lies awake for a long time, the usual advice is to get up, go to another room and do something calm until sleepiness returns, since lying there fretting teaches the brain to associate the bed with alertness. Ravi tried it once on a cold Wednesday, sat in the kitchen with a book and a blanket, and was back in bed within twenty minutes.

Before going to bed, Ravi began to write a short list of the tasks that awaited him tomorrow, transferring them from his restless head onto paper where they could safely wait. One small study found that people who did this fell asleep a little faster than those who simply wrote about the day just gone, although more research would be welcome. The ritual cost him only five minutes, and he decided that it was a bargain worth keeping.

If Ravi woke in the night, which still happened now and then, he no longer looked at the clock, since the sight of a small hour only intensified the calculations of how little sleep remained. He breathed out slowly, rested his muscles and reminded himself that one poor night is unpleasant but not a disaster, because the body is quite good at making up the difference. The rule worked better than he had any right to expect, and the clock gradually lost its power over him.

Meera made one final point, which was that if trouble sleeping continues for weeks, or comes with loud snoring or gasping, a person should see a doctor, since help is available. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, a structured talking programme, has good evidence behind it and is often recommended before sleeping tablets. Ravi, whose nights had improved from five hours to six and then to seven, glanced at his diary and allowed himself a small, tired smile.

Ravi tallied a typical working day in his diary and was a little shocked by the result, which included five cups of coffee, a bag of crisps from the vending machine and a large glass of wine in the evening. None of it was dramatic, but each item was quietly pushing his body in the wrong direction. Meera, when he showed her the list, did not scold him but merely raised an eyebrow.

Caffeine is a stimulant that works by blocking a chemical which normally builds up in the brain and makes us feel sleepy. It can also speed up the heart, cause jitters and nudge up the body's own stress hormones, so that the fifth cup of coffee can feel uncomfortably like a small alarm. Moderate amounts are fine for most adults, and many health agencies suggest staying below about 400 milligrams a day, roughly four cups of brewed coffee.

On average it takes the body about five to six hours to clear half of the caffeine from a cup of coffee, although the figure varies widely from one person to another. That means that a late afternoon latte may still be circulating in the blood at bedtime, quietly sabotaging the first hours of sleep. Ravi moved his last coffee to noon and noticed within a week that falling asleep had become easier.

Alcohol may feel relaxing in the first hour, since it slows some of the brain's activity, but it tends to disturb sleep, especially during the second half of the night. Many people also notice a wave of anxiety the following day, and regular drinking can make stress harder to bear instead of easier. Ravi's Friday glass of wine became a Friday cup of tea, and he did not regret it as much as he had feared.

Nicotine is a stimulant that raises the heart rate and blood pressure, and the calm that smokers feel is largely the relief of a craving that the previous cigarette created. Quitting can feel stressful at first, but many people report that their stress levels fall in the longer term, and a doctor or pharmacist can offer support and treatments. Ravi, who had never smoked, mentioned it only because a colleague had asked him about it.

When people skip meals, their blood sugar can dip, and the result is often shakiness, irritability and a fog that makes small problems seem larger than they are. Regular meals that include some protein, fibre and slow-burning carbohydrates help to keep mood and energy steadier through the day. Ravi noticed that his afternoon headaches, which he had blamed on the children, disappeared almost completely when he stopped skipping lunch.

Ravi resolved to eat lunch at a proper table, away from his desk, his screen and the pile of marking. Eating slowly and without distractions helps the body to shift into its rest-and-digest mode, which is the territory of the vagus nerve and the calming system. His lunch break, previously a hasty ten minutes, expanded into twenty pleasant minutes that cost him nothing and gave back a great deal.

In some studies, even mild dehydration has been found to lower mood and concentration and to make people feel more tired and tense. The evidence is not dramatic, but it is easy to act upon, since drinking water costs almost nothing and is entirely free of side effects. Ravi placed a large bottle on his desk where it would catch his eye whenever he glanced up from his work.

Comfort eating is a thoroughly human response to pressure, and there is no reason to feel ashamed of it, since sweet and fatty foods bring a brief and genuine sense of relief. The honest truth, however, is that no single food, drink or supplement has been proven to cure stress, and herbal products can interact with medicines, so it is wise to ask a doctor or pharmacist first. Ravi stopped looking for a miracle ingredient and simply tried to eat a little more fruit.

After a week of small swaps, such as a coffee cut-off at noon, a proper lunch and an evening cup of tea instead of a glass of wine, Ravi looked at his diary with interest. His scores had slipped from sevens to fives, which was not a transformation but was undeniably a trend. He turned the Body card face down on the desk, feeling that it had earned its rest, and picked up the Mind card.

Meera picked up the Mind card and explained the central idea of the next part of the plan, which was that thoughts are not facts, though they can still start the alarm. A gloomy thought, however mistaken, can send the same chemical messages around the body as a real danger would. If this is true, she said, then the way a person talks to themselves is a form of health care.

Ravi noticed a thought that returned most nights in the small hours, telling him that he was a terrible teacher and that everyone would soon find out. He watched, as if from a distance, how this single sentence led to a sinking feeling and then to a pounding heart and a tight chest. The chain was remarkably tidy, and seeing it written in his own handwriting made it feel less like a fact and more like a habit.

Cognitive behavioural therapy, usually shortened to CBT, rests on the idea that how we interpret events shapes how we feel and what we do. It is among the best-studied talking therapies in the world, and it has good evidence behind it for anxiety, low mood and stress, although it works better for some people than others. Ravi learned that a few of its simple techniques could be borrowed for everyday use, without replacing proper therapy for anyone who needs it.

Meera described some common thinking traps that psychologists have named, including catastrophising, which means leaping to the worst possible outcome, and mind-reading, which means assuming that you know what others are thinking. Others include all-or-nothing thinking, in which things are either perfect or a disaster, and the endless use of the word should. Ravi underlined the words always and never in his diary, since they appeared in nearly every gloomy thought.

Meera taught him a three-step habit, which was to catch the thought, check it and, if necessary, change it. To check it, he could ask himself what the actual evidence was, whether he was jumping to a conclusion and what he would say to a friend who had the same thought. It was a kind of cross-examination, and Ravi found that most of his gloomy thoughts collapsed quickly in the witness box.

The aim was not to force positive thinking, which feels false and which the mind often rejects, but to find a thought that was both realistic and kind. Instead of I am a terrible teacher, Ravi tried this is a hard week, but I have handled hard weeks before, and he noticed that his shoulders dropped a little at the second version. It was a small shift, and small shifts, repeated daily, were precisely what the plan was made of.

Writing about worries and feelings for ten or fifteen minutes at a time helps some people to make sense of them, and a good deal of research has been done on the idea. The evidence is mixed, with benefits that are often small, and it is sensible to stop if the writing leaves a person feeling worse instead of lighter. Ravi tried it on three evenings, and found it useful for two of them and merely tiresome on the third.

Another technique is to set aside a short worry time each day, perhaps fifteen minutes at five o'clock with a kitchen timer ticking beside you. When a worry appears at any other hour, you jot it down and promise to return to it, which, strangely, often loosens its grip. Ravi was astonished that most of the worries lost their urgency by the time the appointment arrived, and the timer rang with nothing left to discuss.

Meera pointed out that worries come in two kinds, which are those that concern a real problem that can be acted upon and those that concern imagined scenarios that may never occur. For the first kind, the best medicine is one small, concrete step, such as sending the email or making the call, while the second kind can be acknowledged and set aside. Sorting each worry into one pile or the other was, Ravi discovered, a surprisingly freeing exercise.

Ravi began to experiment with speaking to himself in the voice of a kind coach in place of a harsh critic, a change that felt peculiar at first, like writing with the wrong hand. Research suggests that self-compassion is linked with lower stress and better coping, and it does not make people lazy, because encouragement tends to work better than scolding. By Friday, the critic had grown noticeably quieter and the coach slightly more confident.

Meera suggested mindfulness, and Ravi, who equated stillness with wasted time, regarded the idea with a raised eyebrow. It sounded to him like sitting on a cushion and doing nothing while the marking multiplied in the next room. She smiled and said that the doing nothing was precisely the difficult part, and that he should try it before judging it.

Mindfulness, Meera explained, means paying attention to the present moment on purpose and without judgement, noticing sensations, sounds and thoughts as they arise. It does not mean emptying the mind or feeling blissful, both of which are practically impossible, and it certainly does not mean never being busy. Ravi was relieved, as he had believed that he would be expected to float away on a cloud of serenity.

The simplest practice, Meera said, was to sit comfortably for five minutes and rest attention on the breath, feeling it come and go at the nostrils or the belly. When the mind wandered, as it was certain to do, he was to notice where it had gone and then gently bring it back, like a puppy that has strayed from its lead. That act of returning was not a failure of the practice, she told him, but the practice itself.

Mindfulness courses, usually lasting eight weeks, have been studied extensively, and they show modest benefits for stress, anxiety and low mood that are broadly similar to those of other well-established methods. They are not a cure, and the quality of the research varies, which is why Meera asked Ravi to treat mindfulness as one tool among many and not as a philosophy to be adopted in a rush. He found that the modesty of her claims, and her refusal to oversell, made him trust her all the more.

Mindfulness is not right for everyone, and some people find that sitting quietly brings difficult memories or feelings to the surface. If a practice causes strong distress, it is wise to stop and talk to a doctor or a trained therapist, who may suggest a gentler approach or a different method altogether. Ravi was glad to find that the honest warnings were part of the instructions and not buried in small print.

Mindfulness, it turned out, did not require a cushion or a special room, since it could be practised during almost any ordinary activity. Ravi paid attention to the warmth of the mug in his hands, the feeling of water on his fingers at the sink, and the way his feet met the pavement on the walk to school. These tiny acts of noticing seemed absurdly simple, and yet he arrived at school feeling calmer than he usually did.

Meera shared a grounding exercise for moments when the mind was spinning, in which a person names five things they can see, four they can touch, three they can hear, two they can smell and one they can taste. The point was to drag attention out of the whirlwind of thought and into the solid, immediate world of the senses. Ravi tried it on a crowded train, and by the time he reached the taste he had almost forgotten why he had been anxious.

On Wednesday morning Ravi tried one quiet minute with his class before the first lesson, asking the children to listen carefully to every sound that they could hear in the room and outside the window. To his surprise they were remarkably good at it, and when the minute ended Sam reported, with great seriousness, that he had heard a pigeon walking on the roof. The class settled more quickly afterwards than it had done at any other point all term, and Ravi wondered why he had not tried it earlier.

Meera suggested another small habit, which was to write down three good things at the end of each day, however minor, and to say briefly why each one had happened. Studies suggest that this kind of gratitude practice lifts mood slightly in some people, though the effect is small and some find it forced. Ravi's first list contained a warm bus, a joke from Sam and a croissant, and, after a week, he found himself noticing good things in advance.

Meera made a final point, which was that some stress, and some difficult feelings, could not be removed by any technique, and that struggling against them often added a second layer of strain on top of the first. It helped, she said, to remember that feelings rise and fall like waves, so that even a very large one eventually breaks and fades. Ravi marked the Mind card as done, with the verdict that mindfulness was a small tool and not a miracle.

The third card, Life, was about the load itself and not just about how Ravi carried it, and he began with the most obvious culprit, which was the mountain of marking. It had been sitting on his desk for so long that it seemed to have acquired a personality, rather like a large and disapproving cat. Meera reminded him that the best calming tool in the world cannot do the marking, and that some stress is solved only by changing the circumstances.

Ravi split the enormous pile into small stacks of ten books and put a sticky note on each, giving every stack a name and a time. A task that feels impossible as a whole often feels possible in slices, and the brain, which dislikes vague and shapeless jobs, responds well to a clear first step. By the end of the evening three stacks had vanished, and the mountain, to his surprise, looked rather more like a hill.

Each morning he now chose the three most important tasks for the day and wrote them on a card, with the rest of the long list pushed deliberately into the background. A short list is far more likely to be finished than an endless one, and the satisfaction of crossing off all three sent a small and welcome signal of success to the brain. Done, he reminded himself, is often better than perfect, particularly at eleven o'clock at night.

Ravi drew two overlapping circles on a sheet of paper, one for the things he could control or influence and one for the things he could not, such as the weather, the inspector's opinion or another person's mood. Into the first he poured his effort, and the second he tried to treat with acceptance, which was easier said than done. Even so, the act of sorting was calming in itself, since it reminded him that most of his worries belonged in the smaller circle.

When Tom asked him to run the school book fair, Ravi felt the old reflex rise to say yes, because saying no had always made him feel guilty and ungrateful. This time he said, warmly, that he could not take it on this term, though he was happy to help for an hour on the day. Tom simply nodded and said that this was fine, and Ravi was amazed that the sky had not fallen.

Ravi gathered his courage and told Mrs Hale, in her sunny office, that his workload had become too heavy and that he wanted to deal with it before it affected the children. She listened without interrupting, thanked him for being honest and moved one of his duties to another teacher who had more time. It was a lesson that asking for help is a skill and not an admission of failure, and that people often respond better than we fear.

Short breaks through the working day appear to help people recover and keep their focus, and the research suggests that even a couple of minutes can make a difference. Every hour or so, Ravi stood at the window, stretched, looked at something far away and let his eyes rest from the page. He had assumed that breaks wasted time, but he found that they gave him more of it, because he made fewer mistakes afterwards.

Ravi set himself a limit, which was to stop marking at seven in the evening and to turn off work email notifications until the next morning. Research links the feeling of being always on call with higher stress and poorer sleep, and he suspected that the children would not suffer from a teacher who was rested. At first the silence in the evenings felt strange, like a house after a party, but he gradually learned to enjoy it.

Constant streams of news and notifications can keep the alarm system primed, and some studies link heavy consumption of alarming news with a worse mood and more anxiety. Staying informed is worthwhile, but it does not require being informed every minute, so Ravi decided to check the news twice a day and to keep his phone in a drawer in the evening. He read an entire paperback in a week, which he had not done in two years.

Ravi was careful to remember that some stressors, such as money worries, poor housing, discrimination or the care of a sick relative, are far too large to be solved by breathing exercises alone. The tools in his notebook can help a person to cope, but they are no substitute for practical help, fair treatment and a society that shares the load. Anyone struggling with such problems might start with a trusted advice service or a doctor, and need not carry them alone.

On Saturday morning Ravi finally met his old friend Dev for coffee, something that he had postponed for two months because of a vague feeling that he had nothing cheerful to report. He hesitated over his first sentence, then decided to be honest and told Dev how stretched and tired he had been feeling. Dev listened without interrupting and then admitted that he had felt much the same for most of the year.

Study after study has linked good relationships with better coping, better health and longer lives, although it is hard to prove that friendship itself is the only cause. A good listener does not need to fix anything or offer clever advice, because simply being heard is often enough to loosen the grip of a worry. Ravi left the cafe feeling lighter, which seemed absurd given that nothing had changed except that two people had spoken honestly.

Dev suggested that it helps to tell a friend what kind of support you need, whether that is practical advice or simply a pair of ears and a cup of tea. Most friends are glad to be asked, he said, because they often feel helpless watching someone struggle and welcome a clear instruction. Ravi tried it by text that same evening, and his sister replied with a row of thumbs and an offer to bring soup.

Dev's dog, Biscuit, bounded across the garden and landed on Ravi's lap with an expression of boundless confidence, and Ravi found himself laughing out loud for the first time in weeks. Laughter brings a brief relief from worry, and some studies link stroking a friendly animal with lower stress and a slower heart rate, though the research is modest. Ravi reflected, with a grin, that Biscuit was quite possibly the cheapest and most cheerful stress treatment that he had ever encountered.

Calm, slow music has been shown in several studies to lower the heart rate and ease stress for many listeners, and singing, whether alone or in a choir, seems to help in a similar way. The effect depends partly on taste, so that one person's soothing melody is another person's irritation, and the best advice is to choose music that you love. Ravi made himself an evening playlist of gentle songs and discovered that he had forgotten how much he liked listening to music.

A hobby that absorbs us completely gives the mind a proper rest, because attention that is fully occupied has no room left to spare for worry. Ravi dug out an old sketchbook that he had last touched at university and spent an hour sketching a bowl of fruit, rubbing out far more than he kept. The result was not good, but it did not matter, because for sixty minutes he had thought of nothing except shape and shadow.

A regular evening routine, made of a few simple and repeated steps, sends the body a clear signal that the working day is over and the time for rest has begun. Ravi tidied his desk, dimmed the lamp and made a cup of herbal tea, always in the same order, until the sequence itself began to make him feel calmer. Habits, he learned, are built from small cues that the brain comes to recognise and trust.

Resilience, Meera explained, does not mean being tough or never struggling, and it is built from many small ordinary habits together with supportive relationships. Like a muscle, it can be developed over time, although unlike a muscle it responds best to kindness and rest rather than to relentless training. Ravi pinned a weekly habit chart to the kitchen wall and ticked off the small things that he did, which made the whole plan feel visible.

After a long period of pressure the body needs genuine rest, and resting is part of the work of recovery, not a reward that has to be earned or a sign of weakness. Ravi spent an entire Saturday morning on the sofa with nothing planned, a blanket over his knees and a book that he did not finish, and he found, with some surprise, that the guilt he had expected never arrived. It occurred to him that tiredness had been his body's way of asking for this.

A really bad Tuesday returned, with a difficult meeting, a lost lunch break and a stress score of eight, and for one evening Ravi felt discouraged and wondered whether any of it had worked. Then he looked at his diary and saw that, over several weeks, the scores had drifted downward from sevens and eights towards fives, with a few bumps along the way. Progress, he realised, is rarely a straight line, and a bad day is a bump, not a collapse.

Meera was careful to say that tools alone are sometimes not enough, and that there is no shame in discovering this. If stress lasts for weeks, interferes with sleep, work or relationships, brings on panic attacks or leads a person to drink heavily to cope, it is time to see a doctor. Ravi wrote this on the Life card, in capital letters, so that he could not argue with himself later.

Stress, anxiety, low mood and burnout overlap in many ways, and from the inside they can feel confusingly alike. Only a trained professional can tell them apart, and the distinction matters because the best treatments differ, but nobody needs to have worked out a label before asking for help. Ravi found this a comfort, since he had been a little afraid that he would be told that he was exaggerating.

Ravi telephoned the surgery and booked an appointment with his doctor, Dr Reyes, and he spent a little time that evening writing a short list of what he wanted to say. The list included his racing heart, his sleep, his headaches, his mood and his worries about work, since doctors can only help with what they are told. It struck him as odd that he could talk to a roomful of children without a moment's hesitation, yet found this simple phone call so difficult.

Dr Reyes listened without hurrying, asked a series of careful questions about his sleep, his work and his habits, and checked his blood pressure and pulse. A doctor may also arrange simple tests to make sure that nothing else, such as a thyroid problem or low iron, is behind the symptoms, since several medical conditions can feel like stress. Ravi found the whole appointment less frightening than he had feared, and rather more human.

In general terms, a doctor may discuss a range of options with a person who is struggling, including talking therapies such as counselling or CBT, stress management programmes and, in some cases, medicines for anxiety or depression. These choices depend entirely on the individual, which is why they must be made with a professional, and medicines should never be started or stopped without medical advice. Many people find that talking with a trained counsellor, week by week, helps them to understand and change their patterns.

Sometimes pressure becomes so heavy that a person begins to think about ending their life or harming themselves, and that is a medical emergency, not a failure or a weakness. If this ever happens to you or to someone you know, contact your local emergency number or a crisis helpline straight away. Tell someone you trust, stay in the company of other people, and remember that these feelings can and do pass with the right help.

To help someone else who seems to be struggling, notice any change in them, ask kindly how they are really feeling and then listen without hurrying to fix everything. Encourage them to talk to a doctor or a counsellor, offer to go with them if that would help and call the emergency services at once if you believe that they are in danger. Ravi thought of Dev, and resolved to ring him that evening, just to ask.

A month later, on another Monday morning, Ravi still felt the familiar surge of nerves before his first lesson, because the reset had not removed stress from his life and was never meant to. What had changed was his response, for he breathed out slowly, dropped his shoulders and reminded himself that the feeling was a tool and not an enemy. By Friday the week looked less like a storm and more like a stretch of ordinary weather.

That Monday night, a month after the Sunday that had started everything, Ravi lay in bed and noticed that his heart was calm and his breathing was slow. He reviewed what he planned to keep, which was the long out-breath, the daily walk, the wind-down hour, the honest conversations and the habit of saying no kindly. Each of them belonged to Body, Mind or Life, and none of them was dramatic, and together they had changed the shape of his weeks.

Ravi closed his notebook, glad to know that stress is a normal part of life and that there is much we can do to keep it in balance. This book has offered general information only, and the science of stress is still developing, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace a doctor who knows you. If you are worried about your own health, please speak to a medical professional, and then take one slow, easy breath out.
